paragraphs: The Senate had passed the amendment in April 1864, but it stalled in the House until Lincoln pushed for a second vote after his re-election. On 31 January 1865 it cleared the House 119 to 56, a margin so tight it needed several Democrats to cross the aisle, and the chamber erupted when the result was read.

Ratification followed within the year: the required twenty-seven of thirty-six states approved it by 6 December 1865, and it was proclaimed law twelve days later. It abolished slavery and involuntary servitude nationwide except as punishment for crime, a clause still argued over in prison labour cases today.

When the amendment was ratified on 23 January 1964, five states still charged a tax at the ballot box for federal elections: Alabama, Arkansas, Mississippi, Texas and Virginia. The fee itself was often small, but registrars paired it with literacy tests and other hurdles that fell almost entirely on poor and Black voters.

The amendment's reach stopped at federal races; it said nothing about state and local elections, where several of those states kept charging the tax. It took a Supreme Court ruling two years later, Harper v. Virginia State Board of Elections in 1966, to strike poll taxes down everywhere else on equal protection grounds.

The revolt that ended Umayyad rule in 750 was not led by an Abbasid at all. Abu Muslim, a commander of uncertain origins operating out of Khurasan in what is now northeastern Iran, raised an army under the black banner and marched west, defeating the last Umayyad caliph at the Battle of the Zab.

The Abbasid family took the throne Abu Muslim had won for them and, within a few years, had him killed as a threat to their own authority. Their capital did not move to Baghdad immediately either: the caliph al-Mansur founded that city in 762, twelve years after the dynasty itself began.

The agreements took their name from the patriarch shared by Judaism, Christianity and Islam, a framing chosen to present the normalisation as broader than a narrow diplomatic deal. Neither the UAE nor Bahrain had fought a war with Israel, so the accords formalised trade and travel ties rather than ending open conflict.

Representatives signed on the Truman Balcony of the White House on 15 September 2020: Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, UAE foreign minister Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and Bahraini foreign minister Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani. Morocco and Sudan reached similar arrangements with Israel in the following months.

The story gives no reason for the move beyond a command: to leave his country, his kindred and his father's house. Terah had already taken the family as far as Haran, in upper Mesopotamia, before dying there. Abram, then said to be 75, continued south with his wife Sarai and his nephew Lot, ending the journey at Shechem in Canaan, where he built an altar.

No document, inscription or excavation from this period names Abraham; the account survives only in Genesis, written down long after the events it describes. What it records is a promise rather than a conquest: land for descendants not yet born, sealed later by circumcision when Abraham was said to be 99. Three faiths trace their founding claim to that promise rather than to any battle or treaty.

Scotland came to the table poor. A failed colonial venture on the isthmus of Panama, the Darien scheme, had swallowed roughly 150,000 pounds of Scottish investment, and England had just barred Scottish exports under the 1705 Alien Act unless Edinburgh negotiated union. Scotland's Parliament had also threatened, in 1704, to pick a different monarch than England's chosen Hanoverian heir.

Union came with a price tag: a payment of about 398,000 pounds, called the Equivalent, covered Scotland's share of a joint national debt and reimbursed Darien's investors, while pensions and offices went to peers and MPs whose votes carried the Act. From May 1707 the two parliaments became one, sitting at Westminster under Queen Anne, and Great Britain existed as a single kingdom for the first time.

The 1798 Irish rebellion, backed by a French landing that came close to succeeding, convinced London that a separate Irish parliament was a standing invitation to future revolt. A first attempt to merge the parliaments failed in the Irish Commons by five votes; a second vote in 1800 passed 158 to 115 after the government distributed peerages and honours to buy support.

The merged Parliament of the United Kingdom first sat on 22 January 1801. Many Irish Catholics had backed union on the understanding that full emancipation would follow quickly, but George III blocked it, and Catholics did not gain equal political rights until 1829, nearly three decades later.

The body it replaced, the Organisation of African Unity, had spent nearly four decades focused on ending colonial rule and apartheid. Once both goals were achieved, its member states judged it too weak to tackle poverty, conflict and trade, and set about drafting a successor with real institutions.

The African Union launched on 9 July 2002 in Durban, with former South African president Thabo Mbeki as its first chairperson. It borrowed structural features from the European Union, including a rotating summit chair and an assembly of heads of state, aimed at closer economic and political integration across the continent.

Alfred took the throne of Wessex in April 871 because his brother Aethelred had just died worn down by fighting the Danes, not because anyone had planned it. His nephews were too young to rule, and with Viking armies already loose in the kingdom, no one contested his claim.

The early years gave little sign of greatness. Alfred lost at Wilton that same spring and had to buy peace, and in January 878 a Danish force under Guthrum caught him off guard at Chippenham, driving him into hiding among the marshes of Athelney. He rallied local levies from there and defeated Guthrum's army at Edington that May.

Four men led the meeting in Bloemfontein on 8 January 1912: lawyer Pixley ka Isaka Seme, writer Sol Plaatje, minister John Dube and Walter Rubusana. All came from South Africa's small class of educated, mission-schooled professionals, and their new congress drew together chiefs and delegates from across the country's Black communities.

Its early strategy was petitioning colonial and imperial authorities rather than confrontation. That shifted around 1920, when the organisation, renamed the African National Congress in 1923, turned to passive resistance campaigns against pass laws that controlled where Black South Africans could live and travel.

Joachim von Ribbentrop and the Japanese ambassador Kintomo Mushanokoji signed the pact in Berlin on 25 November 1936, naming the Communist International as the shared enemy. A secret protocol attached to it was aimed more narrowly at the Soviet Union, committing each side to consult if the other were attacked by Moscow and to avoid agreements that would help the USSR.

Italy joined the following year, turning a bilateral deal into the outline of what would become the Axis, and Spain and Hungary signed on in 1939. During the war itself Finland, Romania, Bulgaria, Slovakia, Croatia and the Japanese-backed Nanjing government all acceded, by which point membership had become less an anti-communist pledge than a declaration of allegiance to Berlin and Tokyo.

Two years before anyone landed on it, the moon already had legal protection. The Outer Space Treaty was opened for signature on 27 January 1967 in London, Moscow and Washington simultaneously, and entered into force that October, months before any crewed mission left Earth orbit.

Its core clauses bar signatories from placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit or on any celestial body, and they forbid any state from claiming sovereignty over the moon or planets by occupation or use. The framework has held for decades without a major violation, even as more nations gained the means to launch.

Congress drafted the Articles while still fighting the Revolutionary War, finishing in November 1777, but getting all thirteen states to ratify took more than three years. Maryland held out longest over western land claims and did not sign until February 1781, just months before Yorktown ended the fighting the confederation had been formed to manage.

The document it produced deliberately kept the new central government weak. Congress could ask states for money but not tax anyone directly, could not regulate trade between states, and any amendment needed every single state's consent. Those gaps left Congress unable to pay its own soldiers reliably and pushed delegates toward the Constitutional Convention six years later.

For forty years ASEAN operated without a founding legal document, run on informal consensus among its members rather than binding rules. Decisions came from summit communiques, not treaty text, which let disputes over sovereignty and non-interference simmer without any mechanism to force a resolution.

Leaders signed the Charter on 20 November 2007 in Singapore, and it entered into force the following December once Thailand deposited the last ratification. It gave ASEAN its own legal personality for the first time, letting the organisation sign agreements and hold institutions accountable in its own name.

Cold War anxiety, not economic ambition, brought five foreign ministers to Bangkok's Saranrom Palace on 8 August 1967. Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand signed a short declaration meant partly to keep communist influence and outside powers from filling any vacuum in the region.

The Bangkok Declaration committed the five to accelerate economic, social and cultural cooperation and to settle disputes peacefully among themselves. What began as a loose grouping without a headquarters, budget or binding legal structure grew over the following decades into a bloc that now includes ten Southeast Asian states.

Assyria had been a power before and had shrunk before, its territory contracting under weak kings and outside pressure. What restarted its growth from 911 BC under Adad-nirari II was not a single victory but a policy: campaign every year, and treat reconquered land as permanently Assyrian rather than a source of seasonal tribute. His successors kept the pattern going for decades.

The clearest beneficiary was Ashurnasirpal II, who by the 870s BC had pushed Assyrian power to the Mediterranean coast and moved the capital to Nimrud to run it from. Kingdoms that resisted were made examples of, and word of that treatment travelled ahead of the army, which was itself a form of conquest. The empire this built would outlast any one king by more than two centuries.

Cleisthenes did not come to power as a reformer. He lost a factional fight to Isagoras, who called in a Spartan army to expel him, then tried to dissolve Athens's governing council. Ordinary citizens resisted, besieged Isagoras and his Spartan backers on the Acropolis, and forced them out, which is how Cleisthenes returned and got the chance to redesign the constitution.

His main change broke the power of the old aristocratic clans: he replaced four family-based tribes with ten new ones grouped by residence, mixing citizens from coast, city and inland into each. He expanded the governing council to five hundred members chosen by lot, and introduced ostracism, a vote that could exile a citizen for ten years without trial.

Athens's fleet, its one advantage through most of the war, was destroyed at Aegospotami in 405 BC by the Spartan commander Lysander, who then blockaded the grain route through the Dardanelles that the city depended on to feed itself. Starvation, not battle, forced the surrender that followed in April 404 BC, after Corinth and Thebes had already argued for razing the city and enslaving its people.

Sparta refused that demand, citing Athens's part in earlier wars against Persia, but still tore down its fortifications, seized what remained of its navy and dissolved the empire it had built. A Spartan-backed oligarchy known afterward as the Thirty Tyrants took over the city's government, ruling by terror for less than a year before Athenian exiles under Thrasybulus overthrew it and restored democracy in 403 BC.

Roosevelt and Churchill met aboard warships in Placentia Bay, off Newfoundland, in the second week of August 1941, four months before the United States entered the war. What emerged on 14 August was not a treaty either man signed but a jointly telegraphed statement of principles, drafted and redrafted between London and Washington rather than put on paper in one room.

It renounced territorial gain for either country, backed the right of peoples to choose their own government, and called for freed trade, disarmed aggressors and, eventually, a world free of want and fear. Roosevelt would later admit no signed copy of the charter existed anywhere, yet its language shaped the later Declaration by United Nations and the postwar order that followed it.

Philipp Melanchthon, not Martin Luther, wrote the document Lutheran princes brought before Charles V at Augsburg, since Luther was still under imperial ban and could not attend in person. On 25 June 1530 a chancellor read the German text aloud in the bishop's palace, a reading so clear that people outside could hear every word, while the emperor kept the general public shut out.

Charles took months to respond, then rejected the confession that September and gave the Lutheran princes until the following April to submit to Rome's counter-statement. They did not, and Melanchthon wrote a defence of the confession instead, leaving a division between the churches that the meeting had been meant to settle.

The alliance that became the Aztec Empire was born out of a succession dispute, not a plan for conquest. When the Tepanec ruler Tezozomoc died in 1426, his heir Maxtla seized power and turned on his own allies, blockading Tenochtitlan and demanding heavier tribute from neighbouring cities. Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan answered by going to war against his capital, Azcapotzalco, and won in 1428.

Two years later the three victors formalised their partnership as the Triple Alliance, agreeing to share the spoils of future conquests, two shares to Tenochtitlan and Texcoco and one to Tlacopan. On paper the three cities remained equals. In practice Tenochtitlan's own armies grew so dominant that within decades it was the alliance in all but name.

Al-Mansur chose an empty stretch of the Tigris in 762, four years after his family had taken the caliphate from the Umayyads, and reportedly saw no better place for a garrison in his lifetime. Construction of the Round City took four years and, by tradition, more than 100,000 workers. Its plan put the caliph's palace and the main mosque at the centre of two concentric walls, a layout meant to echo paradise as described in the Qur'an.

The site was not virgin ground; older settlements and canals from earlier Mesopotamian empires already ran through the area, which is part of why al-Mansur wanted it. Within a generation the new capital had outgrown the old Sasanian city of Ctesiphon nearby and drawn scholars, merchants and translators from across the region, becoming for a time the largest city in the world.

Indonesia, Burma, India, Ceylon and Pakistan called the meeting that opened in Bandung on 18 April 1955, and twenty-nine governments sent delegates, together speaking for well over half the world's population. None were the Soviet Union or the United States. Zhou Enlai attended for China and struck a deliberately conciliatory tone, easing fears among smaller delegations about Chinese ambitions in the region.

Delegates left with the Bandung Declaration, ten principles on peaceful coexistence and respect for sovereignty that were aimed squarely at colonial rule and at pressure from both Cold War blocs. Indonesia's Sukarno spoke of a bloc of what he called newly emerging forces. The gathering fed directly into the founding of the Non-Aligned Movement six years later.

The government needed 1.2 million pounds to rebuild a navy the French had beaten in 1690, and it had neither the cash nor the credit to borrow it outright. The Scottish trader William Paterson proposed a fix: a joint-stock company would lend the crown the money at 8 percent interest, in exchange for a charter and the right to issue notes against the loan.

Charles Montagu steered the plan through Parliament as the Tonnage Act of 1694, and the money came fast: 1.2 million pounds from 1,268 subscribers inside twelve days. The royal charter followed on 27 July, creating the Governor and Company of the Bank of England as a lender to the state rather than a household name for savers.

Philip II led the Macedonian army against a coalition of Greek city states, chiefly Athens and Thebes, near the Boeotian town of Chaeronea in August 338 BC. His eighteen year old son Alexander commanded the cavalry on one wing. The sides were roughly matched, but the Macedonian phalanx broke both flanks of the Greek line, and Thebes's elite Sacred Band, a unit of 300 men, was reportedly wiped out where it stood.

An Athenian orator later said the freedom of the Greeks was buried with the men who fell there. Philip did not destroy Athens but forced the defeated cities into the League of Corinth, a confederation under his own leadership that ended their independent conduct of war and foreign policy. He was assassinated two years later, and it was Alexander who led the League's planned campaign against Persia.

Antigonus was the last of Alexander's marshals still trying to reunite the whole empire under one ruler, and by 301 BC the others had combined against him. At Ipsus in Phrygia, Seleucus, Lysimachus and Cassander's forces met Antigonus and his son Demetrius. Antigonus, in his eighties, was surrounded by allied infantry and killed by javelins thrown from a distance.

Demetrius fled, and the coalition carved up the territory Antigonus had held. Seleucus took eastern Anatolia, Lysimachus the rest of Asia Minor, and Ptolemy kept Egypt, which he had already occupied without joining the actual fighting. No single ruler would come close to reuniting Alexander's empire again, and the battle set the rough borders of the Hellenistic kingdoms for the next century.

The revolt began at an opera. On 25 August 1830 a Brussels audience watching Auber's La Muette de Portici rose at the duet Amour sacre de la patrie and poured into the streets shouting for revolt against Dutch rule. Within days crowds held the Parc de Bruxelles and the royal palace, and Dutch troops under Prince Frederik fought house to house for four days in September before withdrawing to their fortresses.

The great powers met in London that December and, with none of them willing to send troops to restore Dutch authority, recognised an independent Belgium. Leopold of Saxe-Coburg accepted the new throne and took his oath as king on 21 July 1831, a date still marked as Belgium's national day.

Xi Jinping unveiled the plan not in Beijing but at Nazarbayev University in Astana, Kazakhstan, on 7 September 2013, describing a 'Silk Road Economic Belt' of overland trade routes linking China to Europe. A maritime counterpart, the '21st Century Maritime Silk Road', followed weeks later.

The two strands merged into what became known abroad as the Belt and Road Initiative, financing ports, railways and power plants across dozens of countries through Chinese state loans. Recipient governments took on large debts to Chinese banks, and several later renegotiated terms on projects that ran over budget.

Stalin's blockade was aimed at a currency, not a city. When the Western powers introduced the Deutsche Mark into West Berlin in June 1948, Soviet forces cut every road, rail and canal link to the city to force its withdrawal. Rather than abandon the two million people left inside, Britain and the United States began flying in everything they needed.

The airlift ran for fifteen months, delivering over two million tons of coal, food and fuel across more than 200,000 flights, with a plane landing roughly every thirty seconds at its peak. One American pilot, Gail Halvorsen, began dropping small parcels of sweets to children below, a habit that grew into an organised effort called Operation Little Vittles.

Fourteen states sent delegates to Berlin between November 1884 and February 1885, including the United States and the Ottoman Empire alongside every major European power. Not one African ruler was invited; the Sultan of Zanzibar's request to attend was turned aside under pressure from anti-slavery campaigners who wanted the conference to look otherwise.

The resulting act confirmed King Leopold II's personal claim to the Congo through his International Congo Society and declared free trade along the Congo basin, but its lasting rule was that a claim to African territory needed actual occupation on the ground to be recognised. That single requirement set off a scramble among European powers to plant garrisons across the continent within a matter of months.

James Madison had argued against adding a bill of rights at all, calling the Constitution's structure protection enough. He changed course once it became clear that several states would only ratify with a promise of amendments attached, and he ended up drafting most of them himself in the First Congress.

Congress sent twelve articles to the states in 1789. Ten were ratified by 15 December 1791 and became the first ten amendments. One dealt with congressional pay and went nowhere for two centuries before finally becoming the Twenty-seventh Amendment in 1992; another, on the size of the House, has never been ratified at all.

On the night of 20 June 1756, British and Indian prisoners were shut into a small guardroom at Fort William after the fort fell to the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj-ud-Daulah. A survivor, the East India Company official John Zephaniah Holwell, later wrote that 123 of 146 men died overnight in the heat and crush.

Historians have never agreed on Holwell's numbers. Stanley Wolpert put the total confined closer to 64, with 21 surviving; other estimates suggest a smaller cell and a lower toll. Most agree Siraj-ud-Daulah had not ordered the imprisonment and was unaware of it. The episode nonetheless entered British memory as justification for Robert Clive's later conquest of Bengal.

The territory had no name of its own for most of the war, known simply as Upper Peru, a mountainous appendage of the Spanish empire fought over by armies from Buenos Aires and Lima alike. Antonio Jose de Sucre's campaign broke the last royalist resistance there in 1825, and delegates meeting at Chuquisaca that July had a real choice: join Peru, join Argentina, or stand alone.

They chose independence, and signed the declaration on 6 August 1825, naming the new republic after Simon Bolivar, who had led much of the wider South American struggle from the north. Bolivar was declared its first president but left within months to attend to Peru and Colombia, handing the country to Sucre, who governed it for the next several years.

Pedro was on horseback near a stream called Ipiranga on 7 September 1822 when letters reached him from Portugal, ordering him back to Lisbon and stripping his ministers of authority. He tore the Portuguese colours from his uniform on the spot and told his companions the break was final.

He rode back to Sao Paulo that night to announce it, and was acclaimed Emperor Pedro I within weeks. The declaration did not end the matter: Portuguese garrisons held parts of Brazil for years afterward, and it took until 1825, and a formal treaty, before Lisbon accepted what Pedro had shouted by a riverbank.

The 2016 referendum, decided by a margin of just under four points, only started the process. Article 50 negotiations dragged through three years of parliamentary deadlock in London, two changes of prime minister and a delayed departure date, before the withdrawal agreement was finally ratified.

The United Kingdom left the EU's political institutions at 11pm on 31 January 2020, but stayed inside the single market and customs union under a transition period that ran until 31 December that year. A new trade agreement with the bloc took effect on 1 January 2021.

The Government of India Act received royal approval on 2 August 1858, less than a year after the uprising that began among Company sepoys at Meerut had spread across northern India. It stripped the East India Company of the territories and armies it had ruled for a century, transferring them to the Crown outright. A new Secretary of State for India, answering to Parliament, took over its administration from London.

Queen Victoria was proclaimed sovereign of India the following year, and a viceroy replaced the Company's governor general as the ruler on the ground. The change was framed as correcting the defects in Company government that the rebellion had exposed, rather than as any softening of British authority; Indians remained excluded from the senior ranks of the civil service the act created.

Chief Justice Earl Warren wanted no dissent recorded, and on 17 May 1954 he got a unanimous 9 to 0 ruling. The Court held that separate schools for black and white children could never be equal, overturning the standard set almost sixty years earlier in Plessy v. Ferguson, which had allowed segregated facilities as long as they were nominally comparable.

The ruling itself set no deadline. A second decision the following year told districts to desegregate with all deliberate speed, a phrase vague enough that many Southern states spent years finding ways around it, from closing public schools outright to funding private academies that admitted only white students.

Aung San did not live to see the country he had negotiated free. On 19 July 1947 gunmen burst into a cabinet meeting in Rangoon's Secretariat Building and shot him along with eight of his colleagues, six months before the independence he had spent his life pursuing took effect on 4 January 1948.

Burma also made a choice few other former colonies made at that moment: it left the Commonwealth entirely rather than remain a dominion under the crown. Clement Attlee's government told parliament it regretted the decision, but the Burma Independence Act had already been drafted to allow for a country outside the King's dominions.

Napoleon expected Moscow's governor to hand him the keys to a stocked, sheltering city. Instead the fires began within a day of the French occupation in mid September 1812, and burned for four days. Historians still argue over how deliberate it was, but the governor, Fyodor Rostopchin, had ordered the fire brigades removed before he left.

Roughly two thirds of the city's residential buildings were destroyed, along with hundreds of churches, though enough structures survived that a French general judged there was still room for the whole army. What Moscow lacked was food and forage. Napoleon waited five weeks among the ruins before abandoning the city in October, starting the retreat that broke his army.

Caesar's first crossing in 55 BC nearly failed at the beach. His legionaries hesitated to jump into deep water under British spears until, by one account, the standard bearer of the Tenth Legion leapt in first rather than let the eagle fall into enemy hands. Storms then wrecked part of his fleet, and after a few weeks with little gained he withdrew, though Rome still granted him twenty days of public thanksgiving.

He returned the following year with 800 ships and five legions, pushed inland across the Thames, and beat the British leader Cassivellaunus, who had staked the riverbank against him. Cassivellaunus agreed to pay tribute and Caesar left a client king, Mandubracius, in charge of the Trinovantes. No Roman garrison stayed behind; actual conquest waited another century, for Claudius.

James Marshall spotted flecks of metal in the tailrace of a sawmill he was building for John Sutter on 24 January 1848, and tried at first to keep it quiet. Word got out anyway, and by 1849 close to ninety thousand people had crossed oceans, deserts and mountain passes to reach the diggings, splitting almost evenly between sea and overland routes.

San Francisco grew from roughly a thousand residents to twenty-five thousand within two years, and the territory drafted a state constitution before Congress had even settled how new land should divide over slavery. For the Native peoples of California the migration brought displacement, disease and killing on a scale some historians now call genocide.

Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin spent thirteen days at Jimmy Carter's presidential retreat in Maryland, from 5 to 17 September 1978, in talks so tense that Carter reportedly kept the two leaders apart for much of it and shuttled between their cabins himself.

The result was two framework agreements, one sketching a broader Middle East settlement and one specifically for Egypt and Israel, signed at the White House. The bilateral framework led directly to the Egypt-Israel peace treaty the following March. Sadat and Begin shared the 1978 Nobel Peace Prize, though much of the Arab world condemned Egypt for negotiating alone.

Canute's claim to England was not inherited but fought for. He landed at Sandwich in 1015 with roughly 200 ships and spent fourteen months harrying Wessex and Mercia before the decisive Battle of Assandun on 18 October 1016, where an English commander's withdrawal mid-battle helped decide the day against Edmund Ironside.

Canute and the wounded Edmund then met on an island near Deerhurst to divide the kingdom, Canute taking the north and Edmund the south, with the whole to pass to Canute on Edmund's death. Edmund died weeks later, on 30 November, and Canute was crowned in London the following year, later adding Denmark and Norway to his rule.

The Carolingian line had not run out of heirs when Hugh Capet became king in 987. A cousin, Charles of Lower Lorraine, was still alive and had a claim, but he had made himself a vassal of the German emperor and the great lords of France would not accept him. Meeting at Senlis after King Louis V died childless, they chose Hugh instead, on the argument that a throne need not pass by blood alone.

Hugh was crowned twice within five weeks, at Noyon on 1 June and again at Paris on 3 July. That same year he had his own son Robert crowned as co-king, a precaution against exactly the kind of disputed succession that had just put him on the throne. The house he founded held the French crown, through cadet branches, for close to nine centuries.

Daniel O'Connell forced the issue by winning a County Clare by-election in 1828 that he legally could not take his seat from, since Catholics were barred from Parliament by oath. His Catholic Association had organised rent collections and rallies drawing crowds in the tens of thousands, and the government feared what refusing him might trigger in Ireland.

The Duke of Wellington, no friend of Catholic rights, pushed the Act through anyway in 1829 and even threatened to resign over it, judging civil unrest the greater danger. Robert Peel, once nicknamed Orange Peel for his opposition, backed him. The same Parliament raised Irish voting property qualifications, cutting the Catholic electorate it had just enfranchised.

When Pepin the Short died in 768, the Frankish kingdom did not pass to one heir but to two. Charlemagne was crowned at Noyon and his younger brother Carloman at Soissons on the same October day, and for three years the brothers ruled jointly, each holding separate Frankish territories rather than sharing one throne.

That arrangement ended when Carloman died suddenly in December 771. Charlemagne moved at once to take control of his brother's lands rather than let them pass to Carloman's young sons, and from that point ruled the Franks alone, the position from which he built an empire across most of Western Europe.

When Maximilian I died in 1519, the imperial title went to election by seven German princes rather than by inheritance, and Charles stood against Francis I of France and even Henry VIII of England for it. He won on 28 June 1519, helped by heavy payments to the electors arranged through the Fugger banking house.

Frederick of Saxony, an elector himself and briefly a candidate, turned the contest by declining the crown and speaking for Charles instead, arguing that only a ruler of Charles's resources could resist the Ottomans. The election joined Spain, the Netherlands, Austria and the Empire under one crown, though coronation as emperor still lay ahead.

Charles's claim to Spain ran through his mother, Joanna of Castile, who was still alive when her father Ferdinand II of Aragon died in January 1516. Rather than wait, Charles had himself proclaimed king jointly with Joanna, an awkward arrangement given her legal claim, and the Castilian parliament at Valladolid only grudgingly accepted it in 1518.

He was sixteen and had grown up in the Netherlands, barely speaking Castilian when he arrived to take up the crown. The union of Aragon and Castile his grandparents Ferdinand and Isabella had built now passed to a Habsburg who would, within three years, add the Holy Roman Empire to his titles as well.

Chile's independence was declared on 12 February 1818, but the date on the document mattered less than the army that could defend it. Bernardo O'Higgins had led the Patria Vieja resistance years earlier; it took Jose de San Martin marching an army across the Andes from Argentina to give the declaration any teeth.

That army was tested at Maipu on 5 April 1818, when patriot forces broke the last major royalist push against central Chile. Spain refused to recognise any of it for another quarter century, and pockets of royalist resistance in the south held out until 1827, but Maipu is what made the February declaration stick rather than read as another failed attempt.

For over two decades the Republic of China on Taiwan held China's seat at the United Nations, even as the Communist government in Beijing controlled the mainland. Albania led a group of seventeen member states pressing to correct what they called an anomaly rather than a genuine representation of China.

On 25 October 1971, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 2758, recognising the People's Republic of China as the sole legitimate representative of China and expelling the Taipei delegation. Beijing took both the Assembly seat and the permanent seat on the Security Council, a shift several NATO members and non-aligned states had voted to support.

Getting into the World Trade Organization took China fifteen years of negotiation, longer than almost any other member's application. Talks stalled repeatedly over tariffs, state subsidies and market access, and Beijing had to agree to cut import duties on hundreds of categories of goods before members would sign off.

Membership took effect on 11 December 2001. Foreign firms gained new rights to sell directly into Chinese markets and Chinese exporters gained protection from arbitrary tariffs abroad, a trade that reshaped global manufacturing over the following decade far more than either side had projected at the signing.

Southern senators held the floor for 54 working days trying to talk the bill to death, Robert Byrd alone speaking for fourteen straight hours. Senator Richard Russell said openly that his side would resist to the end any measure bringing about what he called social equality. On 10 June 1964 the Senate voted 71 to 29 to cut off debate, the first time cloture had ever succeeded against a civil rights filibuster.

President Lyndon Johnson signed the bill on 2 July 1964, weeks after the vote that broke the filibuster. It reached that point only through a bipartisan rewrite led by Senators Mansfield, Humphrey, Dirksen and Kuchel, which pulled in enough Republican votes to survive the Southern bloc. The law banned segregation in public accommodations and schools, and discrimination in hiring.

The French civil code took effect on 21 March 1804, replacing a patchwork of feudal, royal and regional law that varied from one province to the next. It banned secret and retroactive statutes, required judges to apply the written law rather than invent new rules from the bench, and was drafted in plain French rather than the Latin of earlier codes.

Napoleon carried the code into the territories his armies occupied, and it outlasted his empire: versions of it still underpin the law of France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Louisiana and much of Latin America. Romania kept a Napoleonic-derived code in force until 2011.

Japan's Tokugawa shogunate had spent two centuries under sakoku, a policy that restricted foreign trade to a single port and a handful of Dutch and Chinese merchants, largely to keep Christianity and outside wealth from unsettling its rule. Perry had first appeared off the coast in 1853 with a show of naval force and left a demand for a reply within the year.

He returned in February 1854 with eight warships, and on 31 March signed the Convention of Kanagawa at what is now Yokohama. Its twelve articles opened two ports to American ships, guaranteed aid to shipwrecked sailors, and promised the United States any terms Japan later granted another power, a small opening that widened fast.

Six separate British colonies, each with its own parliament, tariffs and railway gauge, spent the 1890s arguing over how much power a shared government should hold. Referendums settled the terms, and on 1 January 1901 the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution was proclaimed at Centennial Park in Sydney.

Edmund Barton was sworn in as interim prime minister that day, leading a ministry of nine before any election had been held. Federation kept the colonies as states inside a new bicameral parliament, with a governor-general representing the monarch, rather than dissolving them into one unified administration.

Henry Clay put five bills before the Senate in January 1850, and it was Stephen Douglas who broke them apart and steered each through Congress after Clay's health failed. California entered as a free state, ending Southern hopes of a slave-state belt to the Pacific, while Texas gave up its claim to New Mexico in return for the federal government taking on its debt.

New Mexico and Utah were organised on popular sovereignty, letting settlers vote on slavery rather than have Congress decide, and the slave trade, though not slaveholding itself, was banned in Washington. The compromise's sharpest edge was a strengthened Fugitive Slave Act, which denied accused runaways the right to testify and made helping them a federal crime.

No single document created it. The Concert of Europe grew out of the Congress of Vienna as an understanding among Austria, Britain, Prussia, Russia and later France that the great powers would settle disputes through conferences rather than let any one state upset the borders just redrawn. Its other purpose was blunter: putting down the liberal and nationalist uprisings that kept breaking out across the continent.

It never had fixed rules or a secretariat, just a habit of meeting when a crisis threatened to spiral, and historians argue over exactly when it stopped working. A first phase held roughly until the 1860s; a looser version limped on through rising nationalism and rigid alliance blocs until 1914, when a crisis in the Balkans finally proved too large for any congress to manage.

For fifty years popes and emperors had fought over a single question: who could appoint a bishop. Reformist popes, Gregory VII foremost among them, argued that a secular ruler had no authority to hand a churchman the ring and staff that marked his office. Emperors had done exactly that for generations, treating bishoprics as posts to reward loyal men.

Pope Callixtus II and Emperor Henry V settled it at Worms on 23 September 1122. Henry gave up the right to invest clergy with ring and crosier, leaving that to the Church, but kept a hand in elections and could still grant a bishop his temporal lands with a sceptre, a separate and later ceremony. The papal side put it plainly: the Church would have what belonged to Christ, and the emperor what belonged to him.

Delegates from across Europe gathered in Vienna from September 1814 to redraw the map after Napoleon's abdication, and Austria's foreign minister Metternich ran the show. France arrived defeated and largely excluded, yet Talleyrand talked his way into the inner circle anyway, playing the great powers off one another until France had a seat at the real decisions.

Then, in March 1815, Napoleon escaped Elba and marched on Paris. The delegates kept negotiating anyway, and the Final Act was signed on 9 June, nine days before Waterloo settled the matter for good. Between sessions there were enough balls and banquets that one Austrian diplomat is remembered for joking that the congress danced rather than worked.

Until 1982, changing Canada's constitution still meant asking the British parliament to do it. Ottawa and every province but Quebec reached a deal in November 1981, in a late-night meeting known afterward as the Kitchen Accord, on a formula for amending the constitution at home and a charter of rights to go with it.

The British parliament passed the Canada Act in March 1982, ending its own authority over Canadian law, and Queen Elizabeth II signed the Constitution Act into force in Ottawa on 17 April 1982. Quebec's government, under Rene Levesque, never signed on, a refusal that still shapes arguments over the province's place in the federation.

When Muhammad arrived in Medina in 622, the city held Muslim migrants from Mecca, local converts, pagan Arab clans and several Jewish tribes, none bound to the others by blood or prior loyalty. The document he drew up made membership a matter of shared commitment rather than kinship, naming the signatories one community regardless of tribe.

Its terms let each group keep its own faith and law: for the Jews their religion, for the Muslims theirs, while requiring joint defence of the city and peaceful arbitration of disputes rather than the customary tribal retaliation. Muhammad sat as arbiter over the whole arrangement, a role no single clan chief in Medina had previously held.

The delegates who met at Pennsylvania's State House from late May 1787 were supposed to be revising the Articles of Confederation, not replacing them. Within days they had agreed to start over. Windows were nailed shut against the summer heat to keep the debates from leaking out, and no official transcript survives beyond a secretary's sparse minutes.

George Washington presided over roughly fifty-five delegates, though attendance on any given day was closer to thirty. Rhode Island sent nobody. James Madison's own notes, the fullest record of what was argued inside that sealed room, stayed unpublished until after his death in 1836. Thirty-nine of the fifty-five delegates present signed the finished Constitution on 17 September.

Emperor Constantine convened the bishops at Nicaea in 325 not out of theological conviction but to stop a quarrel splitting his newly unified church. The Alexandrian priest Arius had been teaching that Christ the Son was created by God the Father and therefore not equal to him or eternal, a position that had already caused riots in Egypt.

Roughly two to three hundred bishops attended, and the council sided against Arius, declaring the Son consubstantial with the Father in a creed that anathematised anyone who said there was a time before Christ existed. Arius was exiled, but his teaching outlived the verdict, resurfacing among Germanic kingdoms for centuries afterward.

No bishop from the Western church sat in the Church of Hagia Irene when roughly 150 Eastern bishops gathered there in 381. Theodosius I had called them together to settle disputes Nicaea had left open, and by July they had expanded the Nicene Creed with a fuller statement on the Holy Spirit as giver of life, worshipped alongside Father and Son.

The bishops condemned Arianism, Macedonianism and Apollinarianism in the same sittings, and threw out the contested appointment of Maximus as bishop of Constantinople. One of the council's seven canons also ranked Constantinople's bishop second in honour only to Rome's, a claim that unsettled relations with the older patriarchates for decades.

Cyril of Alexandria opened the council in June 431 before John of Antioch's delegation had even reached the city. Sixty-eight bishops walked in to protest the early start, and Cyril answered by having an imperial decree read out and accepted as covering the proceedings. Nestorius, patriarch of Constantinople, was tried in his absence.

The gathered bishops rejected Nestorius's separation of Christ's human and divine natures and stripped him of his office. They ruled that Mary should be called Theotokos, God-bearer, rather than the narrower title Nestorius preferred. John of Antioch's delegation, arriving late, held its own rival session and condemned Cyril in turn before Rome's legates backed the original council.

Byzantine emperor John VIII Palaiologos travelled to Italy in person, hoping Western military help against the advancing Ottomans could be bought with a reunion of the churches. Negotiations moved from Ferrara to Florence, working through disputes over purgatory, papal primacy and the filioque clause that had divided Rome and Constantinople for centuries.

On 6 July 1439 both sides signed the decree Laetentur Caeli, declaring the schism over. It did not survive the journey home: Constantinople's clergy and public accused the emperor and patriarch of betrayal, and the union was never accepted in the Orthodox east. When the Ottomans took Constantinople fourteen years later, Sultan Mehmed II put anti-union clergy in charge of what remained of the church.

The clay cylinder was buried as a foundation deposit under a temple wall in Babylon and stayed there until Hormuzd Rassam dug it up for the British Museum in 1879. Its cuneiform text is a building inscription in a familiar Mesopotamian form: it damns the deposed king Nabonidus, credits the god Marduk with choosing Cyrus, and describes his entry into the city and his restoration of temples and displaced peoples.

Calling it the first charter of human rights is a twentieth century reading. The Shah's government promoted that phrase in 1971, and a copy still sits at the United Nations, but most specialists treat it as a conventional royal inscription following a much older genre, not a legal or political declaration. What is not disputed is Cyrus's own claim to have returned exiled peoples and their gods to their homes.

Darius's own account, carved into the cliff at Bisotun, says that after Cambyses II died an impostor named Gaumata had taken the throne by posing as Cambyses's brother Bardiya. Darius and six fellow noblemen killed the pretender at a fortress called Sikayauvati in September 522 BC, and Darius took the crown. Historians treat much of that as Darius's justification for what may simply have been a seizure of power from Cyrus's line.

He spent his early reign putting down revolts across the empire before extending it further than any Achaemenid king before him, from Thrace in the west to the Indus valley in the east. His invasion of European Scythia around 513 BC gained little ground, and his attempt to punish Athens for aiding an Ionian revolt ended in defeat at Marathon in 490 BC, six years before his death.

The Bible says the Jebusites who held Jerusalem taunted David that even the blind and lame could keep him out, confident in their walls. He took the city anyway, according to the account by sending men up a water shaft into it. Nineteenth-century excavators found such a shaft and assumed it was David's route in; later study showed it is a natural fissure, not a tunnel dug by anyone.

Jerusalem belonged to neither the northern nor the southern Israelite tribes, which is likely why David wanted it: a captured city with no prior claimant could become his alone. He renamed it the City of David and, by tradition, later brought the Ark of the Covenant there, joining royal and religious authority in one place. Archaeology from this period is thin, so much of the story rests on the biblical text itself.

Germany had defaulted on reparations payments, and in 1923 France and Belgium answered by occupying the Ruhr, Germany's industrial heartland, to seize goods directly. The crisis that followed helped drive German hyperinflation to its worst. An American committee chaired by the banker Charles G. Dawes was called in to break the deadlock rather than punish it further.

The plan Dawes produced, adopted in 1924, lowered Germany's annual payments and staggered them upward over five years, while a foreign loan, much of it raised on Wall Street, recapitalised the German central bank. It eased the crisis without settling the underlying sum owed, and by 1929 a second scheme, the Young Plan, replaced it.

Negotiators shut Slobodan Milosevic, Franjo Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic inside Wright-Patterson Air Force Base near Dayton, Ohio, for three weeks in November 1995, refusing to let them leave until they had a deal. They initialled the agreement there on 21 November and signed it formally in Paris on 14 December, with Bill Clinton, Jacques Chirac and other leaders as witnesses.

The accord split Bosnia and Herzegovina into two entities, a Bosniak-Croat federation and the Serb-led Republika Srpska, joined under a rotating national presidency and a single constitutional court. NATO deployed a sixty thousand strong force to enforce the ceasefire lines it drew, ending nearly four years of war.

The capital's location was settled over dinner, more or less. Alexander Hamilton wanted northern votes for his plan to have the federal government assume state war debts; Thomas Jefferson and James Madison wanted the capital on the Potomac for southern states. The trade became the Residence Act, signed in July 1790, with Philadelphia serving as a ten-year stopgap while the new city was built.

George Washington picked the exact site the following year, a diamond of land straddling the river and taking in Georgetown and Alexandria. Pierre Charles L'Enfant laid out its broad avenues, though he was fired within a year over disputes with the commissioners overseeing the project. The government did not actually move in until 1800.

Alexander died in Babylon on 10 or 11 June 323 BC, the city he intended to make the capital of an empire that stretched from Greece to the Indus. He was 32, and had already been forced to turn his army back at the Beas River in India the previous year when his own troops refused to march further east. He left no adult heir and, according to later writers, no clear instruction for who should succeed him.

Without an agreed successor, his generals, later called the Diadochi, fought a series of wars over the following decades that carved the empire into rival kingdoms in Macedonia, Egypt and across the former Persian territories. His death is usually taken as the start of the Hellenistic period, in which Greek language and culture spread through the lands he had conquered even as his own line was hunted down and destroyed.

Genghis Khan died while still campaigning, in August 1227, during a siege against the Western Xia in what is now northwestern China. Sources disagree on the exact day, giving either the 18th or the 25th, and give no consistent account of the cause. He was around 65.

No successor was named before he died, and the Mongol elite spent two years arguing over the succession while his brother Tolui governed as regent. Not the eldest son Jochi but the third, Ogedei, was chosen in 1229, and it was under him that Mongol campaigns pushed further into China, Persia and eastern Europe.

Augustus had spent decades avoiding the appearance of monarchy while holding power more completely than any king, and he spent just as much care arranging who would follow him. He outlived several chosen heirs before settling on his stepson Tiberius, whom he adopted and had granted powers equal to his own well before the end.

He died at Nola in August of the year 14, reportedly asking those present whether he had played his part well in the comedy of life. Tiberius succeeded him with little disruption, the Senate confirming powers he already held in practice. That smooth transfer, arranged in advance rather than fought over, became the pattern for how the principate would pass from one emperor to the next.

Charlemagne died at Aachen on 28 January 814 and was buried in the palace chapel he had built there. His only surviving legitimate son, Louis the Pious, inherited the whole empire intact, an outcome Charlemagne had not managed for his own father's generation, when Frankish custom usually split land between brothers.

Louis could not hold that unity for his own sons. After years of civil war among them, the Treaty of Verdun in 843 split the empire three ways: Lothair kept a middle strip and the imperial title, Louis the German took the eastern lands, and Charles the Bald took the west, borders that later hardened into Germany and France.

Ali was washing Muhammad's body for burial in Medina when a separate argument broke out at a courtyard called Saqifah. The Muhajirun who had followed Muhammad from Mecca and the Ansar of Medina disputed who should lead the new community, and the meeting turned heated before Umar pledged loyalty to Abu Bakr, who became the first caliph.

Ali's own supporters, including Muhammad's uncle Abbas and companions such as Zubayr, argued he had already been designated at an earlier gathering, Ghadir Khumm, and that Saqifah had bypassed him. That disagreement over legitimacy hardened over the following decades into the divide between Sunni and Shia Islam.

On New Year's Day 1942, the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union and China signed a pledge in Washington to fight the Axis with their full military and economic strength and not to seek a separate peace. Twenty-two further governments added their names the next day, and the tally reached forty-seven by the time the war ended.

Roosevelt had coined the phrase United Nations for the wartime coalition, and this declaration is where the name first carried legal weight rather than serving as a slogan. The commitments it wrote down against separate peace and pooled resources became the basis on which the permanent organisation was built three years later in San Francisco.

Seventeen African territories became independent states in 1960, more than in any other single year before or since. Most had been French possessions, including Chad, Gabon, Ivory Coast and the Republic of the Congo, whose independence days clustered through July and August. Nigeria, by far the most populous of the new states, followed on 1 October.

The pace was set less by any single agreement than by exhaustion on the colonial side and organised pressure on the other: France had already granted its territories self-government in 1958 and found full independence hard to refuse once the first few asked. The wave left several new borders, drawn decades earlier by colonial administrators, essentially unchanged.

Protestant nobles confronted four Catholic regents at Prague Castle on 23 May 1618 over the suppression of their religious rights, then put two of the regents and a secretary on trial on the spot for subverting the emperor's promises. Found guilty within the hour, the three men were thrown from a castle window some fifteen metres above the ground.

All three survived the fall. Catholic writers credited the Virgin Mary with catching them; Protestant accounts later claimed a dung heap broke the landing, though no contemporary source mentions one. The incident tipped Bohemia's Protestant estates into open revolt against Emperor Ferdinand II, opening the Thirty Years' War that spread across Europe for the next three decades.

Qutb ud-Din Aibak had begun life enslaved, bought as a boy and raised in the household of Muhammad of Ghor, whose armies he later commanded in northern India. When Muhammad was assassinated in 1206, Aibak, already governing Ghorid territory from Delhi, took the title of Sultan rather than deferring to a distant heir. Contemporaries called him Lakhbaksh, giver of lakhs, for the generosity he showed his soldiers.

He ruled only four years before dying after a fall from his horse during a game of polo. The dynasty he began, later called the Mamluk or slave dynasty for his own origins, was the first of five that governed from Delhi over the next three centuries: Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi, each seizing the throne from the last rather than inheriting it peacefully.

Sparta had led the Greek war effort at Plataea and Mycale, then lost interest in chasing the Persians further. Athens took over, and in 478 BCE delegates from the Aegean city-states met on the sacred island of Delos to found a new alliance, pooling ships and money to keep fighting Persia and to divide whatever spoils came of it. The League's treasury sat on Delos itself, watched over by Athenian officials.

Membership was not really optional once a city had joined: those that tried to leave were besieged back into line. In 454 BCE the treasury moved to Athens, officially for safekeeping, though Pericles then spent some of it on Athenian building projects, the Parthenon among them. By the middle of the century a defensive alliance had become, in practice, an Athenian empire that collected tribute from its allies.

Diocletian did not carve the empire into two halves in a single stroke. He raised Maximian to co-ruler in 286, then in 293 added two junior emperors, Galerius and Constantius, each titled Caesar under a senior Augustus. Four courts, four armies, one frontier problem each: the empire had grown too large for one man to campaign and administer at once.

The system was built to survive its own founders' retirement. In 305 Diocletian and Maximian stepped down together, letting their Caesars rise smoothly to Augustus. It held for one cycle. When Constantius died in 306, his troops proclaimed his son Constantine emperor on the spot, ignoring the succession plan, and the tetrarchy unravelled into rival claimants within a generation.

Thomas Cromwell spent 1535 sending commissioners around England to value every monastery's income and report on its conduct, a survey called the Valor Ecclesiasticus. Parliament then used the results to close any house worth less than two hundred pounds a year, a first pass through roughly 243 smaller communities before the larger abbeys followed.

Monks and nuns were not simply turned out. Most were offered a pension or a transfer to a surviving house, and from 1538 an ordinary monk could expect around five pounds a year for life, a nun rather less. The land and buildings themselves went through a new Crown office, the Court of Augmentations, and much of the proceeds went straight into paying for Henry's wars in the following decade.

Arcadius and Honorius were both minors when their father Theodosius I died in 395, and neither was capable of ruling on his own. The empire passed to them as two halves, the elder taking the east and the younger the west, each propped up by a military strongman, Rufinus and Stilicho, who soon became rivals rather than partners.

No one at the time thought they had created two empires. Romans still spoke of a single state governed from two courts for convenience, not a dissolved union. Only afterward, as the western court weakened and the eastern one endured for another millennium as Byzantium, did the split of 395 read as the one that never healed.

The British North America Act, passed at Westminster, joined the Province of Canada, split into Ontario and Quebec, with Nova Scotia and New Brunswick on 1 July 1867. Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland stayed out at the time, unconvinced the arrangement suited them, and would join decades later on separate terms.

John A. Macdonald, who had lobbied hard for confederation at conferences in Charlottetown and Quebec City, became the new dominion's first prime minister after elections that August and September. Westminster still controlled foreign policy and constitutional amendment, so the country was not yet independent, a status worked out gradually over the following century.

Dred Scott had been enslaved in Missouri, then taken by his owner into free Illinois and the Wisconsin Territory before being brought back south. He sued for his freedom on the grounds that residence on free soil had already freed him, a claim earlier Missouri courts had upheld for other enslaved plaintiffs.

On 6 March 1857 Chief Justice Roger Taney's opinion went further than the case required: Black Americans, free or enslaved, could never be citizens, and Congress had no power to ban slavery in the territories, which struck down the Missouri Compromise. Two justices dissented at length, and the ruling pushed the country closer to war rather than settling anything.

The Act of Abjuration, agreed in July 1581, released the Dutch provinces from their oath to Philip II on the grounds that a king who oppressed his subjects and violated their rights had forfeited his claim to rule them. Officials were told to strike his name and seal from coins and legal documents and swear new oaths to their own provincial States instead.

It was not, at first, a bid to rule themselves. The provinces offered the crown to Francis, Duke of Anjou, and later courted Elizabeth I of England, who sent troops but declined the throne. Only after both efforts failed, and after William the Silent's assassination in 1584, did the States General settle into governing as a republic rather than hunting for a new king.

Elizabeth I granted the charter on the last day of 1600, to a group of London merchants under the cumbersome title of the Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies. It gave them a fifteen-year monopoly on English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope, backed by the threat of seizing the ships of anyone who tried to compete with them.

What began as a trading venture grew into something closer to a government. By the mid-1700s it kept its own private army, and after the Battle of Plassey in 1757 it started ruling Indian territory directly rather than just trading in it. The Crown did not take that power back until 1858, and the company itself was not dissolved until 1874.

Cassius Dio, writing not long after, thought he knew the real motive: more taxpayers. Only citizens owed certain Roman taxes, so an emperor who made every free man in the empire a citizen also made every one of them liable for revenue that provincials had previously escaped. Caracalla issued the edict in 212 CE, and it applied to free women across the empire as well.

A narrower class, the dediticii, mostly people who had surrendered under treaty or freed slaves branded with a criminal record, were left out. Historians also point to a simpler pressure behind the timing: only citizens could serve in the legions proper, so widening citizenship widened the pool the army could recruit from. Roman law itself had to be rewritten piecemeal afterward to fit provincial custom into rules built for citizens alone.

The document agreed at Milan in February 313 did not put Christianity in charge of anything. Constantine and his co-emperor Licinius extended toleration to every religion, ordering confiscated Christian property returned and compensation paid, but stopping well short of an official state faith. That step waited until 380, under Theodosius I, nearly seventy years later.

It was also never quite an edict issued at Milan. Historians now read it as a letter Licinius sent to provincial governors later that year from Nicomedia, after defeating a rival in the east, repeating terms the two emperors had settled on in person. The meeting behind it was real; the paperwork travelled separately.

Henry IV had converted to Catholicism himself to take the throne, but the edict he signed at Nantes in April 1598 let his former co-religionists worship without being harassed for it. Huguenots could hold public office, keep their own courts and universities, and garrison a number of fortified towns at the crown's expense, though Catholicism stayed the official religion and Protestants still paid its tithes.

It held for nearly ninety years. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685, ordering ministers out of France within two weeks and banning most other Protestants from leaving at all. Roughly 400,000 fled regardless, into England, Prussia and the Dutch Republic, taking skills and capital with them that France did not recover for a long time.

Seven states signed the Stockholm Convention on 4 January 1960 and formed the association that May: Austria, Denmark, Norway, Portugal, Sweden, Switzerland and the United Kingdom, nicknamed the Outer Seven against the EEC's inner six. Britain led the push after deciding it would not accept the deeper political union the EEC's founders wanted.

EFTA's members kept their own tariffs against the rest of the world and simply removed them among themselves, unlike the EEC's shared external wall. The looser design suited Britain, Denmark and Norway only for a while: all three later applied to join the EEC instead, and Britain's 1973 departure from EFTA reshaped an organisation that had been built partly around it.

Egypt agreed to something no other Arab state had accepted: recognising Israel outright. The treaty, signed at the White House on 26 March 1979, followed the Camp David framework and set out Israel's staged withdrawal from the Sinai Peninsula, which it had occupied since the 1967 war, in exchange for a demilitarised buffer and normal diplomatic relations.

The peace cost Egypt its place in the Arab League, which suspended the country from 1979 until 1989 over what other members called a unilateral betrayal of the Palestinian cause. Anwar Sadat, who had staked his presidency on the treaty, was assassinated by Islamist militants in October 1981.

Elizabeth was in Kenya, not London, when she became queen. She and Philip had spent the previous night watching wildlife from a treehouse hotel called Treetops before returning to their lodge on the morning of 6 February 1952, where Philip told her that her father, George VI, had died in his sleep at Sandringham.

She chose to keep her own name rather than adopt a new regnal title, becoming Elizabeth II, and the couple cut short a planned tour of Australia and New Zealand to fly home. There was no coronation for another sixteen months; it took that long to prepare Westminster Abbey and rehearse a ceremony that had not been performed since 1937.

Lincoln issued a preliminary warning in September 1862 and the proclamation itself took effect on 1 January 1863. It applied only to the ten states still in rebellion, naming them individually, and explicitly excluded the loyal border states of Missouri, Kentucky, Maryland and Delaware along with several Union-held counties and parishes in the South.

Lincoln had no authority to free enslaved people anywhere the federal government did not control, so the order reached them only as Union troops advanced; immediate freedom in areas already occupied touched perhaps 25,000 to 75,000 people out of more than three million covered on paper. Roughly 300,000 more, in the exempted areas, gained nothing from it at all.

Marcus Aurelius died in March 180, probably at a military camp on the Danube frontier where he had spent much of his reign fighting the Marcomanni rather than governing from Rome. He was the last of five emperors in a row chosen for ability rather than birth, each adopted as heir by the one before him. He broke that chain himself by leaving the throne to his own son, Commodus.

Commodus was around eighteen and had none of his father's interest in the frontier wars or in governing by committee with the Senate. He preferred gladiatorial combat and left administration to favourites, and his reign is generally reckoned the point at which the stability of the previous century began to unwind. Historians still argue over how much of that unwinding was already under way before he took the throne.

Simon de Montfort had already beaten King Henry III in battle once, at Lewes in 1264, and ruled through a council in the king's name. For his 1265 parliament he went further than any English summons before it, writing to the sheriffs to summon barons and bishops alongside two elected representatives from each county and from a chosen list of towns, ordinary men with no title at all.

It did not save him. Prince Edward escaped custody that May and gathered marcher lords and defectors, among them the powerful Gilbert de Clare. At Evesham on 4 August 1265, a little over a year after the parliament, Edward's men marched under Montfort's own captured banners, and Montfort realised who they were only when it was too late.

Britain and France had nearly gone to war over African territory as recently as 1898. The 1904 agreement traded recognition: France accepted British control of Egypt, Britain accepted French influence in Morocco, and a separate clause guaranteed free passage through the Suez Canal.

Smaller disputes came with it. France gave up fishing rights off Newfoundland's coast, Britain handed over territory in West Africa, and the two sides split spheres of influence in Siam. The document was not a military alliance, and said so, but it opened the door to joint staff talks between the two armies in the years that followed.

Most of the ten states that joined on 1 May 2004 had spent the previous decade rewriting their laws to match EU standards, a condition of membership that touched everything from food safety rules to competition policy. Cyprus and Malta joined alongside eight former communist states from Central and Eastern Europe.

The accession nearly doubled the EU's membership at once, from fifteen to twenty five countries, and added roughly seventy five million people. Existing members negotiated transition periods before workers from the new states gained full rights to move and take jobs elsewhere in the bloc.

On 1 January 1999 the euro existed only as an accounting unit. Banks used it to price bonds and settle trades between member states, but no citizen could hold one: francs, marks and lire stayed in wallets and tills for three more years while exchange rates were locked in place.

Notes and coins did not appear until 2002, when eleven countries retired their old currencies within weeks of each other. Vending machines were converted gradually rather than all at once, with roughly two thirds switched over within the first fortnight, while shops kept dual price tags for months so customers could check new totals against something familiar.

Robert Schuman put the proposal in blunt terms on 9 May 1950: pool French and German coal and steel production under one authority, and war between the two countries would become unthinkable, and in material terms impossible. Coal and steel were the raw materials of armies as much as factories, which was exactly why he chose them.

France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg signed the treaty establishing the Community the following year, placing their heavy industry under a supranational High Authority rather than national ministries. It was a modest arrangement in scope but a new kind of institution, one that member states answered to rather than merely negotiated with.

The European Community had spent years failing to finish the common market its founding treaty promised, blocked by rules that let any single state veto new rules. The Single European Act, signed by member states in February 1986, extended qualified majority voting to most single market legislation, so one government could no longer stall the rest indefinitely.

It took effect in July 1987 and set 31 December 1992 as the target date for a market with free movement of goods, services, capital and people. The act also gave treaty status to foreign policy cooperation between member states for the first time, laying groundwork the Maastricht Treaty would build on five years later.

Mary had already been Elizabeth's prisoner for eighteen years when letters intercepted in 1586 tied her to the Babington Plot, a scheme to kill Elizabeth and put Mary on the English throne in her place. She was arrested while out riding and put on trial at Fotheringhay Castle, where a court of English peers found her guilty of plotting against the queen who held her.

Elizabeth hesitated for months before signing the death warrant, and even afterward tried to claim it had been sent without her final approval. Mary was beheaded at Fotheringhay on 8 February 1587, and Elizabeth had the man who carried out the order to send the warrant imprisoned in the Tower for acting on it.

By July 1794, members of the National Convention who had once carried out the Terror alongside Robespierre feared they would be next on his lists. On 9 Thermidor, 27 July, they had him arrested along with Augustin Robespierre, Saint-Just and Couthon. During the arrest his jaw was shattered, either by a gendarme's pistol shot or, as most historians now think, by his own attempt to shoot himself.

He was guillotined without trial the next day at the Place de la Revolution, unable to speak from the wound. His death ended the Terror's most radical phase and the Convention that had condemned him soon turned on the machinery of denunciation itself, dismantling the committees that had run it.

Count Joscelin II had moved his court away from Edessa itself and spent his energy feuding with the count of Tripoli rather than guarding his frontier. When the Muslim ruler Zengi turned his army on the city in late 1144, Tripoli refused to send help, and Edessa fell to a siege on 24 December.

It was the first of the four Crusader states to be lost, and news of it reached Europe as a shock rather than a distant border skirmish. Pope Eugene III called for a new expedition, launching the Second Crusade in 1146, but its leaders chose to attack Damascus instead of trying to retake Edessa, and the city never returned to Christian rule.

Samaria held out for three years against Shalmaneser V before it fell, and the Assyrian king who began the siege did not live to finish it. Sargon II, who took the throne in the meantime, claimed the credit and the numbers in his own inscriptions: 27,290 people carried off, a figure later scholarship treats as a partial count rather than the whole population.

Deportation was standard Assyrian practice, meant to break resistance by scattering a people and resettling their land with outsiders. Some Israelites fled south to Judah before the city fell; those who stayed mixed with the newcomers and became the community later known as the Samaritans. The deportees themselves left no continuous record, which is how they became known simply as lost.

Nineveh had walls thick enough to drive a chariot along, but the siege that broke it, by Babylonians under Nabopolassar and Medes under Cyaxares, lasted only three months. It began in May 612 BC and ended in August, when the defences gave way and the city was plundered and burned. King Sin-shar-ishkun died in the fighting; one account blames a diverted river for flooding the walls open.

Assyria did not end with the city. The king's brother, Ashur-uballit II, escaped to Harran and kept a rump state fighting for several more years before Babylonian and Median forces finished it off. Nineveh itself was left in ruins so complete that later Greek travellers who passed the mound did not know a city had ever stood there.

Zhu Wen began as a salt smuggler before rising through the ranks that put down Huang Chao's rebellion, the revolt whose sack of Chang'an and Luoyang had already broken the Tang court's authority. From his base at Kaifeng he seized Chang'an in 901, forced the emperor to Luoyang, and had him assassinated in 904.

In 907 Zhu Wen deposed the last Tang emperor, the boy Ai, and took the throne himself as founder of the Later Liang. No single power replaced Tang authority across China. Rival states split the country for the following half century, a period historians call the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms, until the Song reunified most of it in 960.

Emperor Min of Jin held Chang'an as the dynasty's last redoubt after Luoyang had already fallen. In 316 the Han-Zhao state, risen from the northern peoples the Jin court had once ruled, took the city and captured him. He was executed soon after, and Western Jin ceased to exist as a functioning state.

Refugees streamed south across the Yangtze rather than accept the new order, carrying the Jin name with them: settlers in Quanzhou named a local river after it. A surviving branch of the imperial family reconstituted the dynasty at Jiankang, today's Nanjing, opening an Eastern Jin period that left the north divided for centuries.

Abu Abdallah al-Shii spent years among the Kutama Berbers of North Africa before his missionary campaign toppled the Aghlabid rulers of Ifriqiya. In 909 he installed Abd Allah al-Mahdi, who claimed descent from Muhammad's daughter Fatima through her husband Ali, as the first caliph of a new Shia state.

The new caliphate rejected the Sunni caliphs in Baghdad outright, claiming its own line of imams rather than acknowledging theirs. It ruled first from captured Aghlabid territory before building the coastal capital of al-Mahdiyya in 921, and over the following decades pushed east until it took Egypt and moved its court to a new city, Cairo, in 973.

The Fatimid general Jawhar led the invasion of Egypt in 969 against the Ikhshidid rulers, who governed the country while nominally answering to the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad. Resistance collapsed quickly enough that Jawhar's first act as conqueror was to lay out a new capital, al-Qahira, meaning the vanquisher, a name that gave the modern city of Cairo its own.

The Fatimids were Ismaili Shia and had already declared their own caliphate in North Africa decades earlier, rejecting Abbasid religious authority outright rather than merely resisting it politically. Taking Egypt gave that rival caliphate a wealthy, populous base within striking distance of Abbasid territory, and Cairo became its capital for the next two centuries.

Cardinal Wolsey staged the June 1520 meeting near Calais as a festival of excess: a temporary palace of timber and painted cloth covering nearly 12,000 square yards, and feasts recorded as running to thousands of sheep and tens of thousands of eggs across more than two weeks of jousting, banqueting and archery between the English and French courts.

The two kings themselves supplied the meeting's one unscripted moment when Henry challenged Francis to wrestle and lost. Whatever goodwill the spectacle produced did not last: within months Wolsey had brokered an alliance with Charles V instead, who then went to war against France, and the elaborate friendship at Balinghem left no lasting settlement behind it.

Crawford Long removed a tumour from James Venable's neck on 30 March 1842 after putting him under with ether, in a small-town Georgia practice with no audience and no announcement. He kept operating quietly for years, wanting to repeat the results before he staked a claim on them.

That caution cost him the credit.
