William Morton gave a public ether demonstration in Boston in October 1846, four years after Long's operation, and it was Morton's name that spread through the medical press. Only after reading of it did Long start gathering patient affidavits to prove he had done it first.

The Savannah stowed her paddlewheels by eight in the morning on the first day out of Savannah harbour on 24 May 1819, and covered nearly all of the rest of the Atlantic under sail. Her engine ran for roughly eighty hours out of a twenty nine day crossing, closer to a tenth of the voyage than the whole of it.

Liverpool had never seen anything like her arrive on 20 June. Crowds packed the piers and rooftops, and hundreds of small boats came out to look at the smoking ship. She stayed twenty five days while curious visitors, including naval officers, toured her decks, before the novelty proved more profitable as spectacle than as shipping.

Congress chartered the bank for twenty years on 25 February 1791, at Alexander Hamilton's urging, to hold federal deposits and issue a stable national currency. Thomas Jefferson and James Madison opposed it fiercely, arguing that the Constitution gave Congress no power to create a bank and that it would enrich merchants at the expense of everyone else.

Hamilton won that argument, and the bank operated through its full term. When the charter lapsed in 1811, Congress declined to renew it by a single vote in each chamber, and the financier Stephen Girard bought most of its stock and building for his own private bank. A second, larger national bank replaced it in 1816.

Eleven ships left Portsmouth in May 1787 carrying roughly 1,400 people, most of them convicts, on a voyage of eight months to the far side of the world. They reached Botany Bay in January 1788, the site James Cook had recommended eighteen years earlier, only for Governor Arthur Phillip to find it open to the sea, short of fresh water and poorly soiled.

Phillip sailed a few kilometres north and found a deep, sheltered harbour he judged one of the finest anywhere. The fleet moved in and raised the flag at Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788, the date Australia now marks as a national holiday, though for the Eora people already living there it began something very different: dispossession followed within years.

Four lodges, three from London and one from Westminster, chose an alehouse for their founding meeting. On St John's Day, 24 June 1717, their representatives gathered at the Goose and Gridiron in St Paul's Churchyard and elected Anthony Sayer as the first Grand Master.

Sayer was a gentleman of modest independent means rather than a figure of rank, and he later fell into financial trouble and had to be supported by the same charity fund his new Grand Lodge of London and Westminster had set up. A blue plaque near the old alehouse site now marks the spot.

The earliest known canal irrigation was not in the Mesopotamian floodplain itself but nearby, at Choga Mami in what is now Iraq, close to the Iranian border, where channels were diverting river water onto fields by around 6000 BCE. Comparable early systems have been traced to Khuzistan in southwestern Iran around the same period.

Farmers on the Mesopotamian plain proper took up the technique later, from at least the third millennium BCE, building a network of small channels that let them water crops steadily through the growing season rather than relying on seasonal flooding alone. That control over water is what let settlements in the region grow food reliably enough to support cities.

Kadesh itself had settled nothing. Ramesses II and the Hittite king Muwatalli II fought to a bloody standstill around 1274 BCE, and each side went home claiming victory. It took sixteen more years, a change of Hittite king to Hattusili III, and shared fear of a rising Assyria before the two empires finally put the argument on paper.

The tablet found at Hattusa and the hieroglyphic copy in Egypt bind both kings to non-aggression, mutual defence against a third party, and the extradition of refugees and criminals. Each version names the other side's gods as witnesses. Ramesses also married a Hittite princess, and the peace held for roughly eighty years, until the Hittite state collapsed.

In 1744 a local ruler and a wandering preacher struck a bargain in the small town of Diriyah. Muhammad ibn Saud offered Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab protection and armed force; in return, the preacher's strict Wahhabi reading of Islam gave ibn Saud's rule religious backing it had not had before.

Neither man's domain amounted to much on its own. Together their heirs pushed the alliance's territory across the Arabian Peninsula and into the Levant, reaching the coast near Bandar Abbas and the Bab al-Mandab strait, built on the same division of labour struck at the outset: one family supplied the soldiers, the other the doctrine.

The immediate spark was a soldier who displayed his scars in the forum and described losing his farm to a creditor before being imprisoned for debts run up while he fought for Rome. With harsh debt laws still enforced by the consul Appius, plebeians walked out of the city in 494 BC and camped on a hill outside the walls, the Sacred Mount, leaving Rome without the labourers and soldiers it depended on.

The senate had no army without them and negotiated rather than force a return. Some debtors were released from their debts, and the senate agreed to create a new office, tribune of the plebs, elected by plebeians and legally untouchable while in office. It was the first position in Roman government a plebeian could hold, and the secession, a strike rather than a revolt, became the model for at least four later ones.

Samuel Morse chose the words himself, on the advice of a friend's daughter who had picked them from a Bible verse. On 24 May 1844 he tapped them out in his code from the old Supreme Court chamber in the Capitol, and Alfred Vail received them forty miles away in Baltimore.

The line had been built with a federal grant of 30,000 dollars, after years in which Morse struggled to convince Congress the electric telegraph was worth funding at all. Within a decade a tangle of competing telegraph companies covered the eastern United States, and news that had taken days to travel by rail or post could cross a state in minutes.

Cyrus Field had already failed twice, losing cable to storms and snapped lines, before his ships finally joined a cable across the Atlantic floor in August 1858. Queen Victoria and President Buchanan exchanged congratulatory messages that took hours rather than the ten days a ship would need, and New York celebrated with fireworks that set City Hall's roof alight.

The celebration was premature. Chief electrician Wildman Whitehouse pushed excessive voltage through the line trying to speed up transmission, ruining its insulation, and by September the signal had failed altogether after barely three weeks of service. A working replacement did not cross the ocean until 1866.

London, not New York, hosted the United Nations' first working session. Delegates from 51 founding nations gathered at Methodist Central Hall on 10 January 1946, a building better known for church conferences than international diplomacy, because no permanent headquarters yet existed anywhere.

The organisation spent its early years without a fixed home, meeting later in a former World's Fair pavilion in Flushing Meadows before Manhattan construction finished in 1951. That itinerant period included one of the Assembly's most consequential early votes, the November 1947 decision to partition Palestine, taken not in London but at the temporary Flushing site.

Theodor Herzl had wanted to hold the congress in Munich, but Jewish community leaders there, uneasy about a political movement built around a homeland in Palestine, pushed him out. He moved it to Basel instead, where 208 delegates from seventeen countries gathered in the Stadtcasino concert hall from 29 to 31 August 1897.

More than half the delegates came from Eastern Europe, and seventeen women attended, though without a vote. The congress adopted the Basel Program, stating that Zionism sought a home for the Jewish people in Palestine secured under public law, and founded the Zionist Organization with Herzl as its president to pursue it.

Nerva became emperor in 96 with a weak claim and no legions of his own, chosen by the Senate mainly because the alternative to him was chaos after Domitian's murder. His fix was to adopt an heir with real military standing, Trajan, rather than risk a son or a relative. It was a stopgap that hardened into a habit.

Four more times in a row, an ageing emperor adopted a capable outsider instead of naming a blood heir: Trajan chose Hadrian, Hadrian chose Antoninus Pius, and Antoninus chose Marcus Aurelius. Historians later credited the run of adoptions itself with the stability, since each successor arrived with backing already built rather than a court to win over. It ended in 180, when Marcus Aurelius broke the pattern and left the throne to his own son.

Nightingale reached the army hospital at Scutari in November 1854 with 38 volunteer nurses and 15 nuns, to find wounded men lying in filth with barely functioning sanitation. Far more soldiers were dying of typhus, cholera and dysentery than of wounds from battle, and she pressed for handwashing, ventilation and clean supplies against a medical establishment that resisted her.

Death rates at Scutari fell sharply after a government sanitary commission overhauled the sewers and ventilation in 1855, though Nightingale herself credited that broader reform rather than her own efforts. She returned to Britain a public figure and used the attention to reform army medical statistics and found a school for nurses in London.

France had been waiting for a chance to weaken Britain since losing the Seven Years' War, and the American victory at Saratoga in October 1777 convinced Paris the rebels could actually win. Benjamin Franklin, Arthur Lee and Silas Deane signed a treaty of alliance with the French minister Conrad Alexandre Gerard on 6 February 1778.

The agreement bound each side not to make a separate peace with Britain, and it opened the door to French ships, money and soldiers that the colonies could not supply themselves. That support proved decisive years later at Yorktown, where a French fleet closed off the bay while French and American troops besieged the British army on land.

Lafayette drafted an early version with Thomas Jefferson, then the American minister in Paris, looking over his shoulder, before the National Constituent Assembly rewrote it into seventeen short articles and adopted it on 26 August 1789. It swept away noble exemptions from taxation and declared that law applies equally to everyone, a direct answer to a monarchy built on inherited privilege.

The articles said little about who counted as a citizen in practice. Olympe de Gouges would answer with her own Declaration of the Rights of Woman three years later, and slavery in France's colonies was not abolished until 1794, then restored under Napoleon. The 1789 text itself survives largely unchanged, now written into the preamble of the French constitution.

Robert Fulton's North River Steamboat, later remembered as the Clermont, left New York on 17 August 1807 bound for Albany, a distance sailing ships covered unreliably against wind and current. It reached Albany in about thirty two hours of running time, averaging roughly five miles an hour and, by Fulton's own account, overtaking sloops that had been struggling against the wind.

What made the voyage matter was not its speed but its ledger: within its first year the boat turned a profit carrying passengers on a fixed schedule, something no earlier steam vessel had managed. Regular, reliable timing rather than raw novelty was what convinced investors that steam travel on rivers could be a business, not just a demonstration.

Galileo was seventy when he knelt before ten cardinals of the Inquisition in Rome. The formal finding was not heresy itself but that he was vehemently suspected of it, for holding that the sun stands still at the centre of the world and the earth moves. He was made to renounce the view aloud.

The sentence spared his life but not his freedom. Imprisonment was commuted the next day to permanent confinement, and after a spell with an archbishop in Siena he was allowed home to his villa at Arcetri, near Florence, where he lived watched over until his death in 1642.

The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade was meant as a stopgap. Twenty-three nations signed it in Geneva on 30 October 1947 while a much larger body, the proposed International Trade Organization, was still being negotiated among more than fifty countries. When the United States withdrew from that larger project, the stopgap became the only working framework for world trade.

GATT ran on that improvised basis for nearly half a century, through repeated rounds of tariff cuts, before it was finally given a permanent institution. On 1 January 1995 the World Trade Organization took over its functions, and the seventy six governments that had belonged to GATT became its founding members.

Delegates from a dozen European states met in Geneva in August 1864 and signed an agreement built directly on Henry Dunant's proposals from the previous year. It bound signatory armies to spare field hospitals and ambulances from attack and to treat wounded soldiers from any side without distinction once they were disabled from fighting.

Medical staff and the civilians helping them were granted protection as non-combatants, and the treaty gave the red cross on a white ground legal standing as the sign marking anyone and anything covered by these rules. It was the first multilateral treaty of its kind, and every later Geneva Convention was built as an addition to it.

The four conventions adopted in 1949 were written by people who had just read the Nuremberg and Tokyo trial records. Earlier Geneva agreements had covered wounded soldiers and prisoners of war; this revision added a fourth convention protecting civilians, the population that had suffered the war's occupations, sieges and camps with the least legal protection of all.

Together the four texts set out rules for the wounded and sick in the field, the wounded and shipwrecked at sea, the treatment of prisoners of war, and civilians under occupation. Nearly every state in the world has since ratified them, in whole or with reservations, giving them a reach that few other treaties from the period can match.

East Germany did not merge with West Germany as an equal partner. It dissolved itself and joined under Article 23 of the West German Basic Law, the same clause that had let the Saarland rejoin in 1957, and its territory was reconstituted into five states rather than kept as a single unit. The Unification Treaty setting out the terms was signed on 31 August 1990, and unity took effect just after midnight on 3 October.

Full sovereignty still needed the agreement of the four wartime occupying powers, settled in the Two Plus Four Treaty signed that September, which ended Allied occupation rights that had lasted since 1945. Soviet troops did not finish leaving German soil until 1994. East and West Berlin, divided for twenty-eight years, were merged in the same act and Berlin was named the capital of the united country.

Giordano Bruno spent seven years before the Roman Inquisition refusing to recant a list of positions that included denying the Trinity, Christ's divinity and the virgin birth, alongside his belief that souls were reincarnated. He also taught that the universe had no centre and no edge, and that the stars were distant suns with worlds of their own circling them.

The Inquisition burned him alive in Rome's Campo de' Fiori on 17 February 1600 after he refused every chance to recant. Historians still argue over how much his death owed to the cosmology and how much to the theology, since either set of claims alone was enough to convict a man of heresy in that court.

Emperor Charles IV issued the Golden Bull at imperial diets in Nuremberg and Metz in 1356, and it did something no earlier decree had managed: it fixed exactly who could choose the next King of the Romans and how. Seven electors got the vote, the archbishops of Mainz, Cologne and Trier, and the secular rulers of Bohemia, the Rhineland Palatinate, Saxony-Wittenberg and Brandenburg.

Four votes out of seven were enough to elect an emperor, so no minority of three could block a decision forever. The electoral territories themselves were made indivisible, closing off the kind of family partition that had fragmented other German titles. The Bull said nothing about needing papal approval for any of it, a silence that quietly ended Rome's old claim to confirm the choice.

American senator George Mitchell had chaired talks among Northern Ireland's parties for nearly two years before Tony Blair and Bertie Ahern pushed the deal to a close on 10 April 1998. The text split governance into three strands, a devolved assembly in Belfast, cooperation between Belfast and Dublin, and cooperation between Dublin and London, with ministerial seats shared out among unionist and nationalist parties by formula.

Voters north and south of the border ratified it separately in May 1998, in Northern Ireland by 71 percent and in the Republic by 94 percent. Paramilitary groups on both sides agreed to begin decommissioning weapons, and the deal set up an assembly that has been suspended repeatedly since, but the ceasefire it built on has held.

Joseph Paxton was a gardener, not a trained architect, and he sketched the exhibition hall's design on blotting paper during a railway board meeting. His glasshouse of cast iron and glass, nicknamed the Crystal Palace, went from proposal to opening in nine months and enclosed several mature elm trees in Hyde Park rather than cutting them down.

Prince Albert had pushed for the exhibition against sceptics who feared it would draw a mob to London. Instead six million visitors came between May and October 1851, roughly a third of the population of England and Wales, and the profits later paid for the Victoria and Albert, Science and Natural History museums.

An anonymous letter reached a Catholic peer, Lord Monteagle, in late October 1605, warning him to stay away from the opening of Parliament because it would receive a terrible blow without seeing who struck it. He handed it to the authorities, and a search of the cellars beneath the House of Lords on the night of 4 November found Guy Fawkes guarding three dozen barrels of gunpowder hidden under firewood.

Fawkes, a soldier who had spent a decade fighting in the Spanish Netherlands, was arrested under a false name and tortured in the Tower before naming his fellow conspirators. Several, including the plot's organiser Robert Catesby, died resisting arrest at Holbeche House days later; the survivors, Fawkes among them, were convicted of treason and executed the following January.

The dynasty took its name from an obscure ruler simply called Gupta, whose kingdom around 240 was modest. Its real rise came under his grandson Chandragupta I, who took the throne around 320 after marrying Kumaradevi, a princess of the Licchavi clan. That marriage brought territory and prestige enough for him to claim the grand title Maharajadhiraja, king of kings.

What followed is remembered less for conquest than for output. Under Chandragupta's successors, the mathematician Aryabhata worked out a value for pi and described the earth's rotation, while Kalidasa wrote Sanskrit poetry still read today. None of it required a battle: the Gupta court funded scholars and let them work.

Anthony Ashley-Cooper, Earl of Shaftesbury, pushed the bill through a Parliament trying to keep the Catholic James, Duke of York, from the throne, and feared what an unrestrained monarch might do to critics in the meantime. The mechanism it strengthened was old: a prisoner could demand a writ ordering a jailer to bring them before a judge and justify the detention.

What was new was the enforcement. The Act barred jailers from shipping a prisoner abroad or shuffling them between prisons to dodge that writ, and it fined any jailer who tried, with the money going to the prisoner. It covered most criminal detentions, though not treason or felony charges, and left the writ itself as the tool later invoked against arbitrary confinement far beyond England.

Trajan died in August 117 without a clearly named heir, and Hadrian, his cousin and ward, claimed that an adoption had been arranged on Trajan's deathbed. The story was convenient enough, and Hadrian's position as a serving general in the east strong enough, that the Senate had little practical choice but to confirm him.

Where Trajan had expanded the empire, Hadrian spent much of his reign consolidating it, withdrawing from Trajan's unstable Mesopotamian conquests and touring the provinces in person. In Britain he ordered the construction of a fortified wall running roughly 73 miles coast to coast, marking a fixed northern frontier rather than a line for further advance.

Tsar Nicholas II called the conference, and it opened on 18 May 1899, his own birthday, at the House in the Wood near The Hague. Delegates from 26 states banned poison, the killing of surrendered soldiers, looting and collective punishment, and required humane treatment of prisoners.

A separate declaration outlawed dropping projectiles from balloons for five years and banned soft-nosed bullets that flattened on impact, a rule aimed at ammunition nicknamed after the Dum Dum arsenal in India. The conference also created the Permanent Court of Arbitration, the first standing body for settling disputes between states without war.

The Qin state's own capital fell within four years of the emperor's death, and out of the scramble that followed came two rival commanders, Liu Bang and Xiang Yu. Liu Bang, a commoner who had once worked as a minor local official, took the title King of Han in 206 BCE and then finished off Xiang Yu at Gaixia in 202 BCE, becoming Emperor Gaozu of a reunified China.

The dynasty he founded gave China its ethnonym, the Han people, and lasted on and off for four centuries. Under his successors it pushed the Silk Road west, standardised coinage, and produced papermaking and early seismometers. Emperor Wu later made Confucian learning the basis of the civil service, a system for selecting officials that outlasted the dynasty itself by well over a thousand years.

The Hanseatic League never had a founding ceremony, and no single document created it. What happened in 1241 was narrower: Lubeck, sitting on both the Baltic and North Sea trade routes, struck an alliance with Hamburg to protect the roads between them from robbery and tolls. The word Hanse itself would not appear in a document for another twenty six years.

Out of that arrangement grew a network that eventually took in close to two hundred towns across what are now eight countries. Hanseatic ships carried furs, wax, timber and grain west and cloth east, and Bergen's stockfish moved south in exchange for grain. By the time of the Treaty of Stralsund in 1370 the League could fight and win a war against the King of Denmark.

Thirty-five states, nearly every country in Europe alongside the United States and Canada, signed the Helsinki Final Act between 30 July and 1 August 1975. It was not a treaty and carried no enforcement mechanism, only a political commitment covering security, economic cooperation and, in its most contested section, human rights.

Soviet negotiators treated the human rights clauses as a formality that cost them little for Western recognition of Cold War borders. Dissidents inside the Eastern bloc read them differently, and used the accords to found monitoring groups, among them Helsinki Watch, which later grew into Human Rights Watch.

When John of Gaunt died in February 1399, Richard II cancelled the arrangements that would have let his exiled cousin Henry Bolingbroke inherit Gaunt's lands automatically. Richard then left for a campaign in Ireland, and Henry sailed back to England claiming he only wanted his inheritance restored, gathering soldiers and support faster than the king's regents could counter him.

By the time Richard returned, Henry controlled enough of the realm to have himself crowned Henry IV instead, founding the Lancastrian line. Richard was imprisoned and died within months, aged thirty three, most likely starved on Henry's order, though an examination of his skeleton centuries later found no marks of violence.

Henry became king on 22 April 1509 at seventeen, on his father's death, and moved fast once in power. Within weeks he had Richard Empson and Edmund Dudley, his father's unpopular tax collectors, arrested, an early sign of the readiness to use execution as a political tool that would mark the reign.

He also reversed himself on marriage. Having once rejected the idea at fourteen, Henry announced soon after his father's burial that he would after all marry Catherine of Aragon, his brother Arthur's widow, citing a supposed deathbed wish of his father's. The wedding followed on 11 June 1509, with a joint coronation at Westminster Abbey less than two weeks after.

Charlemagne had already been crowned emperor once, in 800, but that title lapsed after his line's power collapsed. When Pope John XII placed a crown on Otto I in 962, he was reviving a defunct office rather than inventing one, giving the German kings a claim to stand as Charlemagne's successors in the west.

Otto had already spent over a decade consolidating power in Germany and northern Italy before the coronation, defeating rival dukes and a Magyar invasion at the Lechfeld. The empire that took shape around his crown had no fixed capital and no single language, a loose federation of princes under an emperor that would outlast most of its neighbours by centuries.

Britain's grip on Hong Kong had always rested on three separate deals: the island ceded outright in 1842, Kowloon added in 1860, and the much larger New Territories held only on a 99 year lease signed in 1898. That lease was due to expire in 1997, and since the colony no longer functioned without the mainland territory attached to it, Britain agreed to hand back the whole thing rather than just the leased part.

The transfer took place at midnight on 1 July 1997, at a ceremony attended by Prince Charles, Tony Blair and Jiang Zemin. China promised Hong Kong could keep its own legal system, currency and way of life for fifty years under the arrangement known as one country, two systems, a promise that continues to shape disputes over how much autonomy the territory actually retains.

On 2 May 1670, Charles II signed away land he had never seen. The royal charter handed a group of London investors, led by his cousin Prince Rupert, exclusive trading rights over every river and stream draining into Hudson Bay, a territory that came to be called Rupert's Land.

Nobody in London had measured what that meant. The drainage basin covered close to four million square kilometres, more than a third of modern Canada, reaching into what is now the north central United States. Rupert became the company's first governor over a territory neither he nor his fellow shareholders had set foot in.

The organisation did not emerge from a labour congress but from a peace treaty. Its founding report was folded into Part XIII of the Treaty of Versailles, adopted at the Paris peace conference on 11 April 1919, on the argument that lasting peace required decent conditions for workers rather than the resentment that had helped produce the war.

Its structure was unusual for the time: governments, employers and workers each sent delegates, though governments held twice the votes of the other two groups combined. The first International Labour Conference met in Washington in October 1919 and adopted six conventions at once, setting limits on working hours and banning most child labour.

By 1493 the empire ruled from Cusco stretched north into what is now Ecuador and Colombia and south along the Andes, held together not by a single army garrisoning it but by the Qhapaq Nan, a road network reaching almost every province it controlled.

Population estimates run from six to fourteen million, a range so wide partly because the Incas kept their records on knotted cords called quipu, most of which the Spanish later destroyed. Households owed labour rather than goods under the mit'a system, which built the roads, bridges and storehouses that made the empire's size workable at all.

B.R. Ambedkar chaired the seven member committee that spent nearly three years drafting the document, sitting through eleven sessions of the Constituent Assembly before it was finished. What they produced remains the longest written constitution of any country, running to 395 articles and eight schedules by the time it took effect on 26 January 1950.

The date was chosen deliberately: 26 January had already been marked twenty years earlier as Purna Swaraj day, when the Indian National Congress first declared full independence as a goal rather than a distant hope. Rajendra Prasad took office as the republic's first president on the same day the document came into force.

A lawyer named Cyril Radcliffe, who had never set foot in India before, was given five weeks in the summer of 1947 to draw the border splitting Punjab and Bengal between two new countries. He worked from out of date maps and census returns, and the line he produced was published only after independence had already taken effect on 14 and 15 August.

Estimates of the dead from the migrations that followed range from roughly 200,000 to two million, a gap that reflects how little the movement of people across the new border was ever formally counted. Between twelve and twenty million people crossed it in one direction or the other, on foot, by cart, and by train.

Andrew Jackson signed the act on 28 May 1830, authorising the government to trade land west of the Mississippi for tribal territory in the southeast. It did not name a single tribe, but its target was the land held by the Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw and Seminole nations, whose removal Jackson framed as an exchange rather than an expulsion.

The Cherokee fought removal in the courts and won a Supreme Court ruling in their favour, which Jackson's administration simply ignored. Federal troops marched roughly 16,000 Cherokee west in the winter of 1838 and 1839 along what became known as the Trail of Tears; thousands died of cold, disease and starvation on the way, one of at least eighteen tribes displaced under the act.

Jawaharlal Nehru and Mohammad Ayub Khan signed the treaty in Karachi on 19 September 1960, alongside a World Bank official whose institution had spent nearly a decade brokering the deal. Rather than sharing each river, the treaty split the Indus system in two: India got the three eastern tributaries, the Ravi, Beas and Sutlej, while Pakistan got the larger western ones, the Indus, Chenab and Jhelum.

The split was lopsided by volume, roughly eighty percent of the combined flow going to Pakistan, but it gave each side clear control rather than a shared tap either could dispute. The treaty survived wars between the two countries in 1965, 1971 and 1999 without either side suspending it, a record that outlasted most of what else the two nations agreed that decade.

Kim Jong Un walked across the concrete demarcation line at Panmunjom on 27 April 2018, becoming the first North Korean leader to set foot in South Korean territory since the Korean War armistice of 1953. Moon Jae-in briefly stepped north in return, a gesture neither side had planned in advance.

The two leaders met at the Peace House inside the Joint Security Area, their first meeting in over a decade, and signed the Panmunjom Declaration committing to work toward denuclearisation and a formal end to the war. Two further meetings between them followed later that same year.

Pope Gregory VII opened the dispute in 1075 with a document, the Dictatus papae, claiming that only the pope could appoint or remove bishops. Henry IV had been doing exactly that across his own territories for years, most recently installing his own choice as Bishop of Milan over Rome's candidate. When Henry refused to back down in 1076, Gregory excommunicated and deposed him.

The argument was never only about religion. German bishops ran much of Henry's administration and supplied troops for his armies, so control of their appointment was control of the empire's machinery, not just its churches. Losing that authority to the pope would have hollowed out royal power at its base, which is why Henry fought a fight that would run, on and off, for nearly fifty years.

Negotiations ran for nearly two years between Iran and six other powers: the United States, Russia, China, Britain, France and Germany. A framework was reached in Lausanne in April 2015, but the harder details, including inspection access, took another three months to finish in Vienna.

Under the deal signed on 14 July 2015, Iran agreed to cut its enriched uranium stockpile by roughly 98 percent and reduce its operating centrifuges from about 19,000 to just over 6,000, in exchange for relief from sanctions once inspectors confirmed compliance. The United States withdrew from the agreement in 2018.

The Anglo-Irish Treaty, signed in December 1921, gave the new state dominion status equal to Canada's rather than full separation, and the Free State itself came into being on 6 December 1922. Members of its parliament had to swear an oath naming both the state and the king, a form of words republicans found impossible to accept and refused to take.

Northern Ireland, six of Ireland's thirty two counties, used a right written into the treaty to opt straight back out the following day, leaving the Free State with the remaining twenty six. A boundary commission was meant to redraw the border afterward, though its work never produced the changes either side expected.

Tariq ibn Ziyad landed at the rock that still carries his name, Gibraltar from Jebel al Tarik, with a force that grew from roughly seventeen hundred men to several thousand as he pushed north in 711. He was a Berber commander acting under Musa ibn Nusayr, sent to test a Visigothic kingdom already weakened by disputed succession.

At Guadalete that July, King Roderic's army was routed and Roderic himself was killed in the fighting. With no rival strong enough to rally the Visigoths, Tariq and Musa's forces pushed on and held more than two thirds of the peninsula within a few years, founding the state later Muslims called Al-Andalus.

David Ben-Gurion read the proclamation at the Tel Aviv Museum on the afternoon of 14 May 1948, and it took him sixteen minutes. The building had no name yet fit for the occasion; it is now called Independence Hall. Within hours the United States had extended recognition, and the Soviet Union followed three days later with formal diplomatic recognition.

Troops from Egypt, Transjordan, Iraq and Syria crossed into the territory the next morning, opening a war that ran into 1949. By its end Israel held about half again the land the United Nations partition plan had allotted it, and more than 700,000 Palestinian Arabs had fled or been expelled from the areas that became Israeli territory.

The Virginia Company's settlers built James Fort on a swampy peninsula in May 1607, choosing the site for its defensible position rather than its water or soil. Both proved bad choices: a severe drought had already begun, and within the first year roughly two thirds of the original settlers were dead before a resupply fleet reached them in 1608.

The worst came later. Through the winter of 1609 to 1610, remembered as the Starving Time, colonists ate dogs, horses and boiled shoe leather, and evidence uncovered by archaeologists shows some resorted to eating the dead. Of the 214 people counted in one supply mission, only 60 survived until a relief fleet under Thomas West arrived in June 1610 and kept the colony from being abandoned.

Sima Yan, Emperor Wu of Jin, had spent years building river fleets before he sent them down the Yangtze against Eastern Wu in 280. The last of the three rival kingdoms surrendered without a prolonged siege, and for the first time since the collapse of the Han dynasty a century earlier, one court ruled the whole of China proper.

The peace did not hold. Emperor Wu's court settled into a decade of prosperity, but his death in 290 left a contested succession that broke into the War of the Eight Princes. Within a generation the unified state he had built was fracturing into the divisions that followed at Luoyang and Chang'an.

Brown expected hundreds of enslaved people to rush to join him once he seized the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, then to fight his way south through the Appalachians freeing more as he went. On 16 October 1859 his small band took the armory with little trouble, but almost no one else arrived, and he let a passing train continue on its way, carrying word of the raid ahead of him.

By the next morning local militia had cut off both bridges out of town, and Brown's men were trapped in the armory's engine house. Marines under Robert E. Lee stormed it on 18 October and captured him wounded. Convicted of treason, he was hanged on 2 December 1859, and became a martyr to abolitionists within weeks of his death.

Charles X gambled that he could rule without an elected chamber's consent. His July Ordinances of 1830 dissolved the Chamber of Deputies, gutted press freedom and barred much of the merchant class from voting, all in one stroke, and Paris answered within two days.

Barricades went up on 27 July, and by the 29th royal troops had lost control of the city, three days that Parisians would call the Trois Glorieuses. Charles abdicated on 2 August and sailed for Britain. The men who had beaten him then bypassed his preferred heir entirely, installing Louis Philippe as a constitutional king instead of a restored absolute one.

The new emperor was seven years old when he was enthroned in Beijing on 7 February 1661, too young to rule, so his late father had named four regents to govern in his place. One of them, Oboi, spent the next eight years accumulating power and eliminating rivals among the other three.

In 1669, with his grandmother's help, the teenage emperor had Oboi arrested and took personal control of the throne. He went on to put down the Revolt of the Three Feudatories in the south, oversee repairs to the Grand Canal, and manage flood control along the Yellow River, governing for sixty one years in total.

Frank Kellogg, the American secretary of state, and Aristide Briand, France's foreign minister, put their names to an agreement signed in Paris on 27 August 1928, in which the signing states renounced war as a tool of policy. Fifteen nations signed that day, and within a decade the number of adherents had climbed past sixty, drawing in most of the world's governments.

The pact carried no mechanism to enforce itself: it named no penalty beyond withdrawing the treaty's own benefits from a violator, and the United States Senate made clear that ratification bound the country to nothing further. States kept fighting without formally declaring war, a habit the pact did nothing to stop, though its wording later helped shape the postwar legal case against wars of aggression.

Ibn Saud had spent three decades taking Arabia region by region, starting with his 1902 recapture of Riyadh, then Nejd by 1921 and the Hejaz, with Mecca, by 1925. Rather than merge them at once, he ruled Nejd and the Hejaz as separate kingdoms under his own crown for several years, an arrangement that kept older loyalties intact while power stayed with him alone.

On 23 September 1932 he combined the two into a single state, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, with himself as king. The date is still marked as the country's national day. The unification gave the new kingdom control of the Hejaz's pilgrimage cities, a source of both prestige and revenue that oil would not rival for another decade.

Delegates in Kyoto argued for eleven days in December 1997 before adopting a protocol that gave industrialised countries specific, binding targets for cutting greenhouse gas emissions, ranging from an eight percent cut for the European Union to an allowed increase for Australia. Developing countries, including fast-growing emitters like China and India, took on no binding targets at all.

The United States signed in 1998 but never ratified it, after the Senate voted 95 to nothing against any climate treaty that exempted developing nations. The protocol needed countries responsible for 55 percent of 1990 emissions to ratify before it took effect, a threshold Russia's ratification finally cleared in February 2005.

Puyi was five years old and had no idea what was happening. On 12 February 1912 his regent, the Empress Dowager Longyu, signed the abdication edict on his behalf, a deal brokered by general Yuan Shikai between the collapsing court and the republicans of the Xinhai Revolution.

The new republic let Puyi keep his title and stay inside the Forbidden City with a household and an annual subsidy, and for some time nobody told him his reign had actually ended. He believed himself emperor still, a fiction the palace maintained until his eventual eviction in 1924, twelve years after the edict he never understood he had signed away.

Spain's grip on its American colonies had been slipping for a decade before 1821, ever since Napoleon's invasion of Spain itself left the crown too weak to govern from across the ocean. In Mexico, a former royalist officer named Agustin de Iturbide switched sides, joined forces with insurgents under the Army of the Three Guarantees, and marched into Mexico City that September without a final battle.

Elsewhere the fighting had been much harder won. Simon Bolivar and Jose de San Martin had spent years campaigning across the Andes and the northern coast, and by the early 1820s most of Spanish South America had followed Mexico out of the empire. Spain kept Cuba and Puerto Rico for another seven decades, but its mainland American empire was effectively gone within a few years of Mexico's break.

The alliance signed at Cambrai in December 1508 called itself a crusade against the Ottomans. Its real purpose sat in secret clauses: France, the Holy Roman Empire, Aragon and the Papal States had agreed to carve up Venice's mainland territory between them, alarmed by how far the republic's holdings had spread across northern Italy.

It did not survive its own success. Once Venice had been badly beaten in the field, Pope Julius II grew more worried about French power in Italy than about Venice, and switched sides in 1510. Aragon followed him into a new Holy League against France, and by 1512 the emperor made his own truce with Venice, leaving the coalition that had formed against it in ruins.

Philip II did not need to persuade the Greek cities so much as defeat them first. After crushing Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BCE, he called the survivors to Corinth and offered terms that looked generous on paper: each city kept its own constitution, free navigation, and a promise of no interference in internal affairs, all guaranteed by a common oath.

The guarantee came with Macedonian garrisons at Corinth, Thebes, Ambracia and Pydna, which made refusal difficult. The League's council named Philip supreme commander for a planned invasion of Persia, a campaign his assassination in 336 BCE prevented him from leading. His son Alexander inherited both the title and the war.

Woodrow Wilson had pushed hardest for it at the Paris peace talks, and its covenant was largely drafted by two other men, Britain's Lord Robert Cecil and South Africa's Jan Smuts. The League came into being on 10 January 1920 with an Assembly, a Council and a permanent secretariat based in Geneva.

Wilson won the Nobel Peace Prize for the idea, then watched his own Senate refuse it. Republican opponents led by Henry Cabot Lodge kept the treaty short of the two thirds majority it needed on 19 March 1920, and the United States never joined the organisation its own president had designed.

Franklin Roosevelt signed the act on 11 March 1941, letting the president lend or lease arms and supplies to any nation whose defence he judged vital to American security, rather than sell them outright and demand cash up front. Britain, already stretched thin on foreign reserves under the old cash and carry rule, was the first beneficiary; China followed within weeks, and the Soviet Union after the German invasion that June.

Congress had no simple way to price a loan of destroyers or aircraft, so most of it was never repaid in the ordinary sense. Roosevelt likened it to lending a garden hose to a neighbour whose house was on fire. By the war's end the United States had supplied roughly fifty billion dollars in aid, nearly two thirds of it to Britain and its empire and a large share to the Soviets.

The plebeians had walked out of Rome before, in earlier centuries, to force concessions from the patrician class. In 287 BC they did it again, withdrawing to the Janiculum hill amid debt disputes, and the dictator Quintus Hortensius was appointed to settle it. Ancient writers blamed debt and conscription; some modern historians think rural plebeians were really after a say in distributing land recently won in the Third Samnite War.

Whatever the trigger, the law that ended the standoff removed the Senate's power to veto decisions of the Plebeian Council. Resolutions passed there, called plebiscita, became binding on all Romans without needing senatorial approval. It closed a conflict between the two orders that had run, on and off, for roughly two centuries.

The American Colonization Society had been shipping free and freed African Americans to the Pepper Coast since 1822, an arrangement that suited slaveholders who wanted free Black people out of the country as much as it suited the settlers seeking a fresh start. By the 1840s the society could no longer fund or govern the colony, and Liberia's settlers had to decide whether to go it alone.

They declared independence on 26 July 1847, becoming the continent's first republic, with a constitution modelled closely on the one used in the United States. The Americo-Liberian settlers who led the new state held political power over a much larger indigenous population that had not been consulted about any of it.

John Adams signed the legislation on 24 April 1800, setting aside five thousand dollars for books a moving government would need once it left Philadelphia for the new capital. The whole collection fit into a room in the Capitol: 740 volumes and three maps, ordered from London for members of Congress to consult.

It did not survive the decade intact. British troops burned the Capitol in August 1814 and destroyed most of what had been bought, leaving only a single account book that an officer took as a souvenir and that was not returned to the United States until 1940. Thomas Jefferson sold Congress his own library, nearly 6,500 books, to rebuild the collection the following year.

Neither man was running for president. Stephen Douglas held an Illinois Senate seat that Abraham Lincoln wanted, and since state legislatures still chose senators before the seventeenth amendment, the two campaigned by arguing directly with each other across seven towns between August and October 1858.

Douglas defended popular sovereignty, letting each territory vote on slavery for itself, a position he had built into law with the Kansas-Nebraska Act. Lincoln pressed him on whether that could ever be reconciled with the Supreme Court's Dred Scott ruling. Douglas kept his Senate seat, but newspaper coverage of the debates made Lincoln a national figure within two years.

The treaty was a fallback. Its predecessor, a proposed EU constitution, had been rejected by French and Dutch voters in 2005 referendums, so negotiators stripped out the symbolic language, kept most of the substance, and called it an amending treaty instead of a constitution to avoid another referendum fight.

Signed on 13 December 2007 and in force from 1 December 2009, it created a standing President of the European Council to replace the rotating six-month chair, and a High Representative to speak for the bloc on foreign policy, roles meant to give the EU a more consistent voice abroad.

Seven governments negotiated at Locarno in October 1925: Germany, France, Belgium, Britain, Italy, Poland and Czechoslovakia. The core deal bound Germany, France and Belgium to accept their shared borders as fixed by Versailles, with Britain and Italy standing as guarantors. Germany would not extend the same acceptance eastward, leaving its frontiers with Poland and Czechoslovakia open to future revision.

The arrangement also committed Germany to keep the Rhineland demilitarised. It held for barely a decade: on 7 March 1936 German troops marched back into the zone, and the other signatories issued verbal protest but took no military response. The treaties stayed nominally in force, but the Rhineland's remilitarisation had already made them dead letter.

Robert Livingston and James Monroe went to Paris in 1803 with instructions to buy New Orleans, nothing more. French treasury minister Barbe-Marbois instead offered the entire territory west of the Mississippi. Napoleon had lost interest in a New World empire after an army sent to crush a slave uprising in Haiti was decimated by fighting and disease.

The Americans settled on fifteen million dollars for roughly 828,000 square miles, under three cents an acre, doubling the size of the country without a shot fired. The deal left the new republic with a stake in a struggle it refused to acknowledge: when Haiti declared independence the following year, the United States would not recognise it and backed a trade embargo instead.

Twelve foreign and finance ministers signed the treaty in the Dutch town of Maastricht on 7 February 1992, after talks that folded together separate negotiations on political union and monetary union into one document. It renamed the European Community the European Union and set out a three pillar structure covering the internal market alongside new areas of shared foreign policy and justice cooperation.

The treaty entered into force on 1 November 1993, after Danish voters, who had rejected it in a first referendum, approved a revised version with opt-outs. It also fixed the path toward a single currency, with convergence criteria on debt and inflation that member states would have to meet before adopting what became the euro.

Portugal's foothold in Macau began in 1557 with an annual rent of 500 taels of silver paid to local Chinese authorities, a lease that outlasted the Portuguese empire that granted it and nearly every other European colony in Asia.

The formal handover came at midnight on 20 December 1999, two years after Hong Kong's return to China under a similar arrangement. Macau became a Special Administrative Region under a promise of separate laws and a market economy for fifty years, the same model applied across the border.

Nobody signed Magna Carta. King John pressed his seal into wax at Runnymede on 15 June 1215, since a medieval king authenticated a document that way, not with a signature. A council of twenty five barons was set up to make sure he kept to it. He did not, and within ten weeks Pope Innocent III had annulled the charter, tipping England into the First Barons' War.

The document that mattered was not the one at Runnymede. It was reissued in 1216 stripped of its sharpest clauses, again in 1217 as part of a peace settlement, and again in 1225 by Henry III in exchange for a new tax grant. Edward I confirmed it as statute law in 1297, and it was that later, revised text, not John's, that entered English law.

Thomas Malthus published his essay anonymously in 1798, arguing that population, left unchecked, doubles roughly every twenty five years while food supply grows only by fixed amounts each cycle. The gap between the two, he wrote, would always be closed eventually by famine, disease or war, whatever policies tried to prevent it.

Darwin later credited the essay directly: reading it in October 1838, he wrote, it struck him at once that favourable variations would tend to survive such pressure and unfavourable ones to perish. Alfred Russel Wallace reached a similar conclusion from the same book, and both built natural selection on Malthus's arithmetic of scarcity.

The men who took Egypt's throne in 1250 had been bought as boys, trained as soldiers, and owed loyalty only to the sultan who armed them. When the last Ayyubid sultan died, his widow and his Mamluk officers moved to keep power within the regiment rather than let it pass to a rival dynasty, ending a family line the Kurdish general Saladin had founded.

For a decade afterward the Franks in the Levant barely noticed them as a threat. That changed at Ain Jalut in 1260, where the Mamluk general Baibars feigned a retreat to draw the Mongol army into a trap and Sultan Qutuz closed it with a flanking charge, the first time a Mongol force had been stopped for good rather than merely delayed.

Japan's Kwantung Army had seized Manchuria by force through 1931, and on 1 March 1932 it proclaimed the territory an independent state, Manchukuo, with its capital at Changchun, renamed Xinjing. To give the new state a face other than a Japanese general's, it installed Puyi, the last emperor of the Qing dynasty, first as regent and later, in 1934, as emperor under the name Kangde.

Puyi signed decrees and held ceremony, but the Kwantung Army's commander doubled as Japan's ambassador and could veto him outright, while Japanese vice-ministers embedded in every department made the actual decisions. Manchukuo issued its own currency and stamps and joined no meaningful international body; only a handful of states, chiefly Japan's allies, ever recognised it.

Marcus Aurelius came to power in 161 on the death of his adoptive father Antoninus Pius, and insisted the Senate name his adoptive brother Lucius Verus as co-emperor alongside him, an arrangement without much precedent. He was already known as a serious student of Stoic philosophy, a habit he kept up through years of war on the Danube and Euphrates frontiers.

His private notebooks, written in Greek during military campaigns and addressed to himself rather than any audience, survived to become the Meditations. He is counted as the last of the rulers later called the Five Good Emperors, a label invented long after his death; his own son and successor, Commodus, broke sharply with the pattern by ruling as an unchecked autocrat.

Facing a shortage of soldiers for the war against Jugurtha in Numidia, the consul Gaius Marius in 107 BC enrolled volunteers from the capite censi, citizens too poor to meet the property qualification that had traditionally governed army service. It was a practical fix for an immediate manpower problem rather than an announced overhaul of the military system.

Later Roman writers credited Marius with far more: redesigning the javelin, making the eagle the sole legionary standard, and reshaping the legion around the cohort. Modern historians doubt most of this, finding little evidence any of it was new or permanent under Marius. What is clear is that opening the ranks to the landless tied soldiers' loyalty to whichever general could reward them with land and pay, a change Marius had not intended.

Isabella, heir to Castile, married in secret on 19 October 1469, without the consent of her half brother King Henry IV. She slipped away from court claiming to visit a tomb in Avila while Ferdinand, heir to Aragon, crossed Castile disguised as a servant to reach her at the Palacio de los Vivero in Valladolid.

As second cousins the pair needed papal dispensation, which they secured through a bull whose authenticity was later questioned, arranged with help from the future Pope Alexander VI. Henry IV denounced the match as a breach of an earlier agreement, but Isabella took Castile's throne in 1474 and Ferdinand inherited Aragon in 1479, and their joint rule became the basis of a unified Spain.

George Marshall chose a Harvard commencement, not a press conference, to announce American aid for Europe on 5 June 1947. He spoke for under twenty minutes and named no figures, leaving the detail to Congress, which eventually voted through roughly twelve billion dollars over four years once Truman signed the programme into law the following spring.

Stalin briefly weighed joining before Molotov walked out of the Paris talks that would have committed the Soviet Union to open its books to American oversight. Moscow then barred the Eastern Bloc from accepting any aid and answered with its own Molotov Plan, calling Marshall's programme a scheme for the economic enslavement of Europe.

Little about Chandragupta's rise is independently confirmed. Buddhist, Jain and Hindu sources agree that he overthrew the Nanda dynasty around 322 BCE with the help of an advisor, Chanakya, but historians treat much of the detail as legend grown up around a real conquest rather than a reliable record.

What is clearer is the scale of what followed: Chandragupta pushed Greek garrisons left behind by Alexander out of the Punjab, then fought his way toward the Nanda capital at Pataliputra, taking territory and installing garrisons as he advanced. The empire he founded eventually stretched from Afghanistan into the Deccan, the first to unify most of the Indian subcontinent under one ruler.

The Mayflower had been chartered for Virginia, but storms pushed it to Cape Cod instead, well outside the territory its passengers had permission to settle. Some of the non-Puritan passengers on board, travelling for their own reasons rather than religious ones, argued that landing outside the agreed patent released them from any obligation to obey Pilgrim leadership.

To head off that argument, 41 of the men on board signed a short compact on 21 November 1620, agreeing to form a body politic and submit to whatever just laws it later passed for the colony's good. It pledged loyalty to James I in the same breath, and gave Plymouth a working government before a single building had been raised ashore.

Behind the restoration lay the domains of Satsuma and Choshu, rivals turned allies who had watched foreign warships force open Japanese ports and decided the shogunate could not be trusted to answer them. On 3 January 1868 their forces backed a declaration that political power was returned to the Imperial House, ending the Tokugawa shogunate that had ruled Japan since 1603.

Emperor Meiji, still a teenager, became the nominal centre of a government run largely by the domain leaders who had put him there. Within a few years the samurai class was dissolved, the old domains replaced with prefectures, and a programme of rapid industrialisation and Western-style institutions was under way.

A ship holding a fixed compass bearing traces a curve on the globe, but on ordinary maps of the time that same course was drawn as a bent line, forcing a captain to keep replotting it. Gerardus Mercator solved this in 1569 by stretching the spacing between lines of latitude further apart the closer they came to the poles, so that any constant bearing became a straight line on paper.

The trade off was size: regions near the poles were inflated far beyond their true area, a distortion still visible in modern classroom maps. Sailors were slow to adopt it, but within a few generations Mercator's projection became the standard chart for ocean navigation, and it still underlies most digital world maps in use.

Independence came not from the insurgents finishing what they started but from a former royalist officer switching sides. Agustin de Iturbide, who had spent years fighting the rebels, joined forces with insurgent leader Vicente Guerrero in 1821 under the Plan of Iguala, and their combined army swept the exhausted colonial government aside within months.

Spain's viceroy signed the Treaty of Cordoba on 27 September 1821, formalising the split. Iturbide then crowned himself emperor of a new Mexican monarchy, a role that lasted barely two years before a republican revolt replaced it with a federal constitution in 1824. Spain did not recognise any of it until 1836.

Zhu Yuanzhang began as a penniless peasant and a Buddhist monk before joining the Red Turban rebels in 1352, during a wave of uprisings against Mongol Yuan rule brought on by heavy taxation and Yellow River flooding that the Yuan government had left unmanaged. He took Nanjing in 1356 and spent the next years crushing rival rebel leaders, most decisively Chen Youliang at the Battle of Lake Poyang in 1363.

With his rivals gone he marched north in 1368, and the last Yuan emperor fled the capital rather than fight. Zhu declared the Ming dynasty and took the era name Hongwu, meaning vastly martial. His rise ended roughly a century of Mongol rule over China and restored a Han Chinese imperial house for the first time since the Song.

Around 2000 BCE, Knossos was already a crowded town, its population estimated to have grown to some 18,000, and sites across Crete including Phaistos and Malia were undergoing major building work as their populations surged. The grand palace complexes people now associate with Knossos followed soon after, going up in the following century or so.

Cretan traders were reaching Egypt, Cyprus, the Levantine coast and Anatolia by this period, carrying goods and styles across the eastern Mediterranean. Later centuries would see that reach grow further still, but the population growth and construction of the centuries around 2000 BCE marked the point at which Cretan society moved from scattered towns toward the networked island culture historians call Minoan.

Bernadette Soubirous was fourteen, illiterate and gathering firewood near Lourdes on 11 February 1858 when she said a woman in white appeared in a grotto at Massabielle. She returned to the site repeatedly over the following months, reporting eighteen apparitions in total, and on one visit in March the figure identified herself as the Immaculate Conception.

During the visions Bernadette uncovered a spring that pilgrims soon credited with healings, and a local bishop formally recognised the apparitions in 1862. Lourdes grew into one of the largest pilgrimage sites in the world, drawing several million visitors a year, and Bernadette was canonised a saint in 1933.

Missouri's request to join the Union in 1819 threatened to tip the Senate's careful balance between slave and free states. The deadlock broke only when Illinois senator Jesse Thomas added a separate provision: Missouri would enter as a slave state, Maine would be carved off from Massachusetts and enter free, and the balance would hold at twelve states each.

Thomas's clause did the lasting work. It banned slavery from the rest of the Louisiana Purchase territory north of the 36 degree 30 minute line, leaving Missouri itself as the one exception north of that mark. The line held for over three decades before the Kansas-Nebraska Act unraveled it in 1854, and the Supreme Court struck it down as unconstitutional in the Dred Scott case of 1857.

Edward I called the Westminster assembly of November 1295 mainly to pay for war, against France, against Scotland, and against unrest in Wales, not out of any theory of representation. He told the summoned lords, clergy and commoners that what touches all should be approved by all, an argument for consent to taxation rather than a plan for a new institution.

The gathering brought together roughly 49 lords and clergy with 292 commoners, two knights from each county and two representatives from each city and borough, a formula later parliaments largely repeated. Historians William Stubbs and Frederic Maitland gave it the name Model Parliament centuries afterward, and it was this assembly's representatives who pressed to trade grants of money for the hearing of grievances.

When Genghis Khan died in 1227 his empire was already twice the size of the Roman Empire at its height. His successors kept expanding it for another two generations. Kublai Khan finished the conquest of Song China in 1279, folding the richest and most populous country on earth into a realm that already ran from Siberia to the edge of Eastern Europe.

By 1294 the Mongol domain covered roughly 23.5 million square kilometres, still the largest contiguous land empire ever assembled under one family. It was never one government for long: within decades of Kublai's death it had split into rival khanates that fought each other as readily as they had once fought outsiders.

President James Monroe delivered the line in his annual message to Congress on 2 December 1823, but the wording was chiefly the work of his secretary of state, John Quincy Adams. It declared the Americas closed to further European colonisation and warned that any attempt to extend a European monarchy's system into the hemisphere would be treated as a threat to the United States itself.

Adams had pushed for a unilateral statement rather than a joint declaration with Britain, wanting the United States to speak for itself even though its navy could not yet have enforced the warning against a determined European power. The doctrine had little practical effect for decades, and it was later presidents, not Monroe, who invoked it to justify direct intervention across Latin America.

Diplomats agreed the Montreal Protocol on 16 September 1987 to phase out chlorofluorocarbons and halons, the refrigerant and aerosol chemicals then widening the hole in the ozone layer over Antarctica each spring. It came into force in 1989, and unlike most environmental agreements it set binding, scheduled cuts rather than voluntary targets, later tightened several times as evidence of the damage grew.

It became the only United Nations treaty ever ratified by every recognised state, with 198 parties. Kofi Annan called it perhaps the most successful international agreement to date, and measurements since have found the ozone layer slowly recovering as roughly 98 percent of the targeted substances were phased out worldwide. A 2016 amendment agreed in Kigali extended the same mechanism to CFC replacement gases.

A white mob rampaged through Springfield, Illinois in 1908, burning Black-owned homes and lynching two men within walking distance of Abraham Lincoln's tomb. The outrage pushed journalist William English Walling, social worker Mary White Ovington and Henry Moskowitz to call a meeting in New York that January.

Sixty prominent Americans signed the founding call, among them W. E. B. Du Bois, Ida B. Wells and Mary Church Terrell. The group formed on 12 February 1909, timed to the centenary of Lincoln's birth. Boston attorney Moorfield Storey, who was white, became its first president, while Du Bois ran publicity and edited its magazine.

George H. W. Bush, Carlos Salinas de Gortari and Brian Mulroney each signed the agreement in their own capital on 17 December 1992, having negotiated it as outgoing or soon-departing leaders. Bill Clinton, who inherited the ratification fight, added side agreements on labour and the environment before pushing it through Congress the following year.

It took effect on 1 January 1994, immediately removing tariffs on roughly half of Mexico's exports to the United States and phasing out most of the rest over the following decade. The deal replaced a patchwork of separate trade rules among the three countries and became the template for the later United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement.

Napoleon sailed from Toulon in May 1798 aiming not at France's usual enemies in Europe but at Egypt, hoping to cut Britain off from its trade routes to India. He brought over a hundred scholars and scientists along with his army, intending to study the country as thoroughly as he conquered it.

The campaign turned quickly. On 1 August 1798, Horatio Nelson's fleet caught the French ships at anchor in Aboukir Bay and destroyed most of them, stranding Napoleon's army in Egypt. The scientists stayed on regardless, and among their finds was a slab of inscribed basalt near Rosetta that would eventually unlock the reading of hieroglyphs.

Twelve countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington on 4 April 1949, building on an earlier and smaller pact among Belgium, France, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Britain. The new treaty pulled in the United States and Canada alongside Portugal, Italy, Norway, Denmark and Iceland, countries with little in common beyond a shared unease about Soviet intentions in Europe.

Its core clause, Article 5, commits every member to treat an attack on one as an attack on all. The wording was deliberately vague about what a response must involve, a compromise that let the United States join a peacetime European alliance for the first time in its history without binding Congress to any automatic declaration of war.

Neanderthals were the first hominins to make Europe a permanent home, present from roughly 243,000 years ago until their disappearance around 40,000 years ago, with a last refuge in Gibraltar perhaps lasting longer still. Their toolkit, known to archaeologists as the Mousterian industry, relied on flaked stone points and scrapers suited to hunting large game.

They kept fire, ate whatever was locally abundant, mostly big game alongside plants and mushrooms, and bore the scars to prove it: their skeletons show frequent fractures from animal attacks and rough terrain. Some groups buried their dead, as at Shanidar Cave in Iraq, though nothing in the graves shows a belief in an afterlife. Their population stayed small throughout, with signs of inbreeding in the surviving remains.

Nero was sixteen when his mother Agrippina, having married the emperor Claudius and arranged for her son to be adopted ahead of Claudius's own son Britannicus, saw Claudius die in October of the year 54. The Praetorian Guard proclaimed Nero emperor that same day, before Claudius's death was even announced to the wider public.

His early years were guided by advisers including the philosopher Seneca, and were later remembered as comparatively restrained. That did not last: Nero had his mother killed in 59, his first wife in 62, and eventually turned on Seneca as well. He died by his own hand in 68 as army commanders turned against him, the last of the Julio-Claudian emperors.

Franklin Roosevelt took office on 4 March 1933 with roughly a quarter of the workforce unemployed and the banking system seizing up under runs. Within days his Emergency Banking Act closed every bank in the country for inspection, reopening only the solvent ones under Treasury oversight, a pause that stopped the panic almost immediately.

Over the following hundred days Congress passed programme after programme: the Civilian Conservation Corps put young men to work planting trees and building trails, the Agricultural Adjustment Administration paid farmers to cut production and raise prices, and the Tennessee Valley Authority began wiring electricity into a region that had gone without it. The pace of that spring gave the whole decade of legislation that followed its name.

Nixon had built his career on hard anti-communism, which made him an unlikely candidate to fly to Beijing. He arrived on 21 February 1972 for a week of talks with Mao Zedong and Premier Zhou Enlai, ending twenty-three years in which Washington and the People's Republic had had almost no direct contact.

The visit produced the Shanghai Communique on 27 February, a statement in which both sides acknowledged deep differences, particularly over Taiwan, while agreeing to work toward normal relations. Full diplomatic recognition did not follow until 1979; what the trip achieved in 1972 was simply reopening a conversation that had been closed since 1949.

Leaders gathered in Belgrade on 1 September 1961 for the first Conference of Heads of State or Government of Non-Aligned Countries, drawing on principles the Bandung Conference had set out six years earlier. Yugoslavia's Josip Broz Tito hosted; Egypt's Nasser, India's Nehru, Ghana's Nkrumah and Indonesia's Sukarno were among the leaders who shaped the founding agenda.

None of the five had any interest in taking orders from Washington or Moscow, and Tito in particular used the movement to keep Yugoslavia's communism independent of Soviet control. The movement never became a formal bloc with binding rules, but it gave dozens of newly independent states a shared platform for arguing against alignment with either Cold War superpower.

Only five states had tested nuclear weapons when the treaty opened for signature in 1968, and the deal it offered was uneven by design. Recognised nuclear powers kept their arsenals for now; everyone else promised not to acquire any, in exchange for help with peaceful nuclear technology and eventual disarmament talks.

It entered into force on 5 March 1970 and now binds 191 states, more than almost any other arms agreement. India, Pakistan, Israel and, later, North Korea never accepted its terms or withdrew from them, and each went on to build a nuclear arsenal outside the treaty's reach.

Delegates from Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela met in Baghdad from 10 to 14 September 1960 and agreed to found the organisation on the final day. The trigger was blunt: multinational oil companies had cut the posted price of crude in 1959 and again that August, without asking the countries the oil came from.

The five founders were answering a market dominated by a handful of Western firms known as the Seven Sisters, who set prices largely on their own terms. OPEC's early role was coordination rather than control; it took over a decade, and several more members joining, before it could move prices by acting together rather than merely comparing notes.

American expansionists had been chanting for the whole of the Pacific Northwest up to the line of 54 degrees 40 minutes, coined as the slogan 'Fifty-Four Forty or Fight'. Britain and the United States had jointly occupied the territory since 1818, and neither government wanted the argument to become a second war.

The treaty, signed on 15 June 1846, split the difference at the 49th parallel instead, the line that already marked the border further east. Vancouver Island stayed entirely British even though the parallel cuts through its southern tip, a compromise that left the boundary running cleanly along the mainland.

Secret talks in Norway between Israeli academics and PLO officials produced a framework neither side's government had put on the table publicly. On 13 September 1993 Yitzhak Rabin and Yasser Arafat shook hands on the White House lawn as Shimon Peres and Mahmoud Abbas signed the actual document, with Bill Clinton presiding.

The accord set up the Palestinian Authority to govern parts of Gaza and the West Bank and scheduled a five year transition toward a permanent settlement, deferring the hardest questions, Jerusalem, refugees, borders and settlements, to later talks. Israel recognised the PLO as representing the Palestinian people, and the PLO recognised Israel's right to exist, but the deferred issues remain unresolved.

Osman I did not inherit an empire. He led a small band of Turkic warriors, the Kayi, in a border region of northwestern Anatolia that his father Ertugrul had held before him, and for years his ambitions ran to capturing individual fortress towns from Byzantine garrisons rather than founding a dynasty. His victory at Bapheus in 1302 was the beylik's first major win against Byzantine forces.

Osman never took Bursa, the city that became his son Orhan's capital in 1326, and he was dead by the time it fell. What he left behind was a working state with its own administration and a reputation for alliances that crossed religious lines, foundations solid enough that his descendants built an empire on them that lasted into the twentieth century.

The papacy needed rescuing before it could be granted anything. When the Lombards seized the Byzantine-held Exarchate of Ravenna in 751, the Duchy of Rome was cut off from Constantinople with no army of its own to call on, leaving Pope Stephen II to look for protection elsewhere.

He found it in Pepin, the Frankish king whom Stephen's predecessor had already crowned in place of the powerless Merovingian line. Pepin marched into Italy, defeated the Lombards, and in 756 handed the former Ravenna territories to the pope rather than keeping them for himself, a grant that gave the papacy direct rule over central Italian land for the next eleven centuries.

The Paris conference in December 2015 succeeded partly by avoiding the mistake of its predecessor: instead of imposing binding emissions cuts from above, as the failed 2009 Copenhagen summit tried, each country submitted its own voluntary pledge and agreed to report progress and revise targets every five years.

Delegates from 196 parties adopted the text on 12 December 2015, committing to keep warming well below two degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, with an aspiration of 1.5 degrees. The agreement entered into force less than a year later, in November 2016, faster than most multilateral treaties manage.

Four parties signed in Paris on 27 January 1973: the United States, North Vietnam, South Vietnam and the Provisional Revolutionary Government representing the Viet Cong. The deal set a ceasefire, required American forces out within sixty days, and allowed prisoner exchanges, but it also let North Vietnamese troops already in the South stay where they were.

That last concession undid the rest. Both sides broke the ceasefire almost immediately, and by March 1973 fighting had resumed in full. Washington did not intervene again; North Vietnamese forces expanded their hold over the next two years and took Saigon in April 1975, ending the war the accords had claimed to settle.

Poland-Lithuania had no army capable of stopping what came next. After the Bar Confederation's rebels lost their fight against Russian influence, Russia, Prussia and Austria simply agreed among themselves to take slices of the commonwealth rather than let any one of them seize it all. Poland's own diet was left to ratify losses it had no power to refuse.

Prussia took Royal Prussia and land along the Notec river, Austria took Galicia along with the salt mines at Bochnia and Wieliczka, and Russia took Polish Livonia and part of eastern Lithuania. Between them the three powers took roughly 30 percent of the commonwealth's territory and about half its population, a first cut that two further partitions would finish within twenty-three years.

Peace is a generous word for it. Augustus's own reign still saw wars on the Rhine and in Spain and the destruction of three legions in Germany's Teutoburg Forest in 9 CE. What the Pax Romana meant in practice was the end of the civil wars that had torn the Mediterranean apart for a century, not an absence of fighting at the empire's edges.

Inside those edges, though, trade moved with unusual freedom: roads, a common currency and a single legal system connected Britain to Egypt without a border crossing between them.
